Every officer or servant of, and every person employed by the company, who wilfully or negligently violates any by-law, rule or regulation of the company or its directors lawfully made and in force, or any order or notice of the board, or of the minister or of an inspecting engineer, of which a copy has been delivered to him, or which has been posted up or open to his inspection in some place where his work or his duties, or any of them, are to be performed. if such violation causes injury to any person or to any property, or exposes any person or any property to the risk of such injury, or renders such risk greater than it would have been without such violation, although no actual injury occurs, is guilty of a misdemeanour, and shall, in the discretion of the court before which the conviction is had, and according as such court considers the offence proved to be more or less grave, or the injury or risk of injury to person or property to be more or less great, be punished by fine or imprisonment, or both ; hut no such fine shall exceed four hundred dollars, and no such imprisonment shall exceed the term of five years. 51 V., c. 29, s. 294 Am.
2. The company may, in all cases under this section, pay the amount of the penalty and costs, and recover the same from the offender or deduct it from his salarv or pav. 51 V., c. 29. s. 295.

Is this an entirely new section ?
181*
No, but there are some changes in the present law which are not material.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: It is simply a farce, because there is no rule or regulation of any railway company in this country which is not wilfully and negligently violated. If this becomes law, it would simply be a farce as it hitherto has been, so long as railway companies are governed by rules and regulations such as they have now.

Suppose the injury resulting from the violation by employees of any of the company's by-laws or rules should result in death, would not this clause clash with the criminal law applicable to the case of manslaughter ?

This law has been in force a number of years, and I do not care to change it. If an employee were indicted for an offence under this clause, his punishment could not exceed that which is provided in it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is a good deal in the contention of the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo. If a man committed the offence described in this section, he would be liable under the common law or the criminal law, even without this section. But the offence proved against him might subject him to a heavier penalty under the criminal law than is provided in this section, and that might cause trouble and confusion.

If an offence were committed which, in the opinion of the crown prosecutor, amounted to manslaughter, the accused would be indicted for that offence under the common law or the criminal code, and if convicted it would be in the discretion of the judge what sentence to impose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But suppose he were indicted for manslaughter and his counsel should contend that he should have been indicted instead for the specific act mentioned in this section ?

No doubt my hon. friend, with his experience of the criminal law, would argue that the accused was not indictable for manslaughter and therefore ought to be discharged. If on the other hand, he was indicted under this section, he could not be punished beyond the penalty therein provided. It would be entirely within the discretion of the crown prosecutor to decide for what class of offence he should be indicted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Section agreed to.

On section 300, subsection 1,

with or without imprisonment, the penalty may, subject to the provisions of this Act, be imposed and recovered on summary conviction before a justice of the peace ; and where the penalty prescribed is more than one hundred dollars and less than five hundred dollars, the penalty may, subject, as aforesaid, be imposed and recovered on summary conviction before two or more justices, or before a police magistrate, a stipendiary magistrate or any person with the power or authority of two or more justices of the peace.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister whether he thinks it prudent to invest two justices of the peace with power of imposing a fine of $500 either against a merchant or against a company or its officers ? It seems to me that this is rather extensive jurisdiction to give to two ordinary justices of the peace.
It is always subject to review. And, of course, $500 is the maximum. I do not know of any other court of first instance to which you could well refer these matters.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would suggest that it be left to the county court judge in each county. I might say that, so far as Ontario is concerned, the justices of the peace are without professional qualification. They only qualify in regard to property, and they never do anything of consequence without consulting the Crown attorney or the county judge.

In Ontario they have a superabundance of county court judges. With us, we have a county court judge for every three, four or five counties. To leave it to the county court judges would not always, therefore, be a very expeditious or convenient manner of enforcing the section.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it is a very dangerous power to give to two justices of the peace. The magistrates may be of a different class in other provinces from what they are in Ontario; they are a very respectable people with us, but I do not think the people of Ontario will be satisfied that two magistrates hearing a case should have power to fine a merchant $500.

There is, as I said, an appeal to a higher court. But after all, I am not sure that you do not confer in some existing legislation equally great powers upon two justices of the peace in other matters. If you were to take the trouble to run over the liquor Acts you will find that very large powers compared with these are conferred upon two justices of the peace. Is it a greater power to enable a justice of the peace to impose a fine of $500 than it is to send-a man to prison ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
A man cannot be sent to prison by a magistrate unless he

consents to be summarily tried by the magistrate. There is no serious offence a magistrate can send a man to prison for, unless the accused has chosen to be tried by the magistrate. Under this section he can without consent. There are some very serious offences a magistrate can try a man for. The Minister of Justice will remember better than I do the crimes for which a magistrate can imprison a man in cases of burglarly and theft and others, but he could not be tried for those cases by a magistrate without his consent. But here there is no option, and there is a penalty of $500. The jurisdiction is absolute, it requires no consent from either party interested. Now the fact is that magistrates can impose a fine of $500, while they cannot put a man in jail for any very serious offence without he has consented to be tried by them instead of going before a higher court, which he would have a right to insist on. But as there is a county court judge in each county who is trying cases all the time in his county, I cannot see why it would not be better to leave this to a county court judge. As to the appeal, X am not sure, looking at this section hurriedly, that there would be the same appeal here there would be in ordinary cases. The only thing that would cause one to think so is that it says ' on summary conviction.' There is no appeal given in this section, yet you are creating a special offence that may not have been contemplated in the Criminal Code, which gives appeals for summary convictions in certain cases. But assuming that there is an appeal, the appeal would go to the county court judge, and why not have it dealt with by him in the first instance ? In regard to what I have said about magistrates, I except the county of Lincoln, where most of them are able and qualified ; but they may not be well qualified in other counties and I am told they are not.

The hon. gentleman has suggested that we should have the county court judge exercise this jurisdiction, and that it should be limited to him. That might apply to Ontario, but not to other parts of Canada. There are no county court judges in some of the other provinces, none in Quebec at all, and none I believe in the Northwest Territories. So you would encumber the thing very much if you undertook to set up different jurisdictions in different provinces.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Could you not use a description that would give jurisdiction to a judge of the lowest degree that is qualified professionally, I mean a judge of the lowest grade who has a legal education ? Could we not use some expression that would apply to that judge in each province ?
The judge of a court of record.
That would make it very awkward in the North-west Territories.

There are various courts of record in the different provinces. I do not think it is so much a question of legal knowledge in these cases, as it is a question of good judgment, and good sense, and a disposition to do what is right; I think those are all the qualifications required. But what the hon. gfentleman has said respecting the powers of justices of the peace to deal with serious cases, does not seem to me to assist us very much in coming to a better understanding- of this matter. It is not a question of the gravity of the offence that has been raised by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), the question is as to the magnitude of the penalty which you are allowing a magistrate to impose. Now my argument was that magistrates are already authorized to imprison for a very considerable period, they are authorized to imprison now, for many offences, for three months, and in some offences for six months -I am not sure that in some cases the term does not go up to a year. I look upon it as being a much graver thing to have power to put a man in prison for a year, or six months, or even one mouth, than it is to impose upon him a fine of from $100 to $500. If the liberty of the individual may be taken from him at the discretion of two justices of the peace, I think you are giving them a very much less serious power when you say that the same magistrates may impose a fine of from $100 to $500. Now it is not an answer to the argument I made, to say that magistrates have no right to deal with serious offences without the consent of the person charged. My argument may be fallacious, but it is not answered by urging that proposition, because, as I say, whether the offence is serious or not, you have given, by your general legislation, to the same number of magistrates, or persons of the same status judicially, the power to do more serious things than to impose a fine. The Minister of Justice has placed in my hands some provisions of the Criminal Code which show just what magistrates may do. They comprise a large class of offences which the magistrate may try in a summary way, and over w'hieh he can exercise jurisdiction without requiring the consent of the accused at all. So that, you see, while at first blush, it may seem to be a somewhat large power to confer upon two justices of the peace, the law of the land confers upon one justice of the peace much larger powders and entitles him to impose more severe penalties.

speechtext: We see every week in the newspapers the returns of traffic and working expenses with regard to the Grand

Every company shall make crossings for persons across whose lands the railway is carried, convenient and proper for the crossing of the railway fqr farm purposes. speechtext: The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) had one or two amendments to propose to this section. He is not here, but he will be here to-morrow. I .think in his absence it would be hardly fair to go on with the section.

On section 196 I have an amendment to propose to meet the requirements of the recent case of the Ontario Lands and Oil Company vs. the Canada Southern Railway Company, which is to be found in volume one, Ontario Reports, 1901, and in which the words ' is carried ' in section 196 are commented upon. It is there held by Mr. Justice Meredith that the words ' is carried ' refer only to railways constructed subsequent to the passing of the Act, and if the section is left in its present form in this Bill the words ' is carried ' would refer only to railways, according to this decision constructed after the passing of this Act. I therefore beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Haldimand and Monck (Mr. Thompson) :
That the words * is carried ' be struck out and that the following be inserted in lieu thereof: ' Which at any time has heretofore or shall hereafter be carried.'
This is to meet the suggestion made by Mr. Justice Meredith, one of the members of the divisional court, whose decision will be found at page 222 of the report previously cited.

speechtext:
Section 197 says :
The company shall erect and maintain, upon the railway, fences, gates and cattle-guards as follows :-
(2.) Fences, of a minimum height of four feet six inches, on each side of the railway, and swing, or sliding gates.
I would like to have the words ' sliding gates ' taken out. The swing gates are all right, but we do not want sliding gates twelve feet in length or shorter, because, when the snow comes in the winter time it is almost impossible for a man and much more for a boy or a girl to open these gates. If they are made to swing on hinges any child can open them, and it is no trouble to shut them, but it is almost impossible for children to open or shut these gates *even in summer time. I would beg of the minister to strike out these words ' or sliding gates.' If he does that he will oblige the people in our section of the country very much.
I am afraid that the hon. gentleman will not find a consensus of opinion in that direction. I know that some people prefer the sliding gates to the swing gates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Perhaps they have not so much snow in your part of the country.
I think we have more snow than you have. I never heard any one complain down our way of a shortage in the supply of snow.

speechtext: This sliding gate is an old-fashioned arrangement, and I do not think it would be any imposition on the railways to make them put proper gates that would swing. Generally the younger members of the family are in charge of the cattle and it requires too much physical force to open and shut these sliding gates. I think the suggestion of the member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinsou) is a good one and I would urge the minister to consider it.

When the cattle guard commission was in St. Thomas the leading farmers of the county of Elgin were summoned to meet them, and these gentlemen objected very strongly to the sliding gates and were as strongly in favour of the gates being put on hinges.

I always considered that the sliding gate was the better gate for the summer, and even when we have snowstorms, if there is a bank of snow against the swing gate you will have to shovel it away before you can open the gate, whereas there would be no such difficulty with the sliding gate.
If you were a practical farmer you would know better than that.

On section 275,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the committee to an amendment which I intend to propose, and I would be very glad to hear if there is any objection to it. This section provides that the railway company shall furnish free transportation on all their trains to the members of the board and such officials as may be indicated by the board, and I propose to add that the same free transportation shall be afforded to members of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada. As a matter of

fact at present I think tliat members of this parliament enjoy free transportation pretty generally if they care to take it, and those who do not enjoy the privilege do not enjoy it because they refuse it, thinking that if they accept it might compromise them in some 'way. As it is done pretty generally and as it would be done universally if all would accept, I think it is desirable that we should state in the Act that this privilege shall be as a matter of right for Senators and members of parliament, so as to remove any feeling of obligation which would otherwise arise. Moreover, we have in the Bill a clause which restricts the giving of passes and the offering of inducements for traffic and all that sort of thing, so that unless we included in some portion of this clause the right that members of parliament should have transportation they might be prevented from getting it. From both these points of view I have been led to suggest to the committee that the clause be changed by adding to the word ' trains ' on the second line the words * for members of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not know whether the minister has considered the members of the provincial legislatures. I think they are in possession of the same privilege if it is a privilege, and for the reason the minister has stated they may be prevented from getting free transportation in future.
I mention that as the minister may have forgotten it.

I have to compliment the minister on placing that clause in the Bill. You may remember that a few years ago I introduced a resolution on the same lines, believing that it was only the right of members of parliament to come to this House of Commons on a pass to discharge their duties. I believe that when we take a pass from the railways we are not under any obligation to them, and I believe that we should get it as a right and not as a matter of grace. However, I think that we should go further and declare that no mileage shall be paid to the members. I hope the minister will find it possible to insert a provision in the Bill that members who come here on passes shall not accept the mileage allowance from the government. Some of the members perhaps will not like this, but I think it would be only fair and just to the country if you would provide that when we get passes from the railway companies we shall not charge mileage to the country.
It would be very hard on some members ; take the member for the Yukon, where there is no railway at all.

You could pay his expenses if there is no railway ; you can provide for him, but you should not
pay a member who travels on a railway on a pass.
You draw the distinction then.
Yes.

I think that so far as the local legislatures are concerned the custom is that the members of the cabinet get free passes. I understand the hon. gentleman's position to be that if we get a pass there should be no mileage.
That is right.
I take it that any gentleman who believes that, does not charge mileage when he takes a pass; we must be consistent.

The objection to free passes on the railways is the temptation to hon. members to absent themselves from their parliamentary duties from time to time. Many of them leave Ottawa on Friday night and return Tuesday morning, while others, whose homes are too far distant to enable them to do this, are here all the time. The time of the session is thus squandered by hon. members availing themselves of the privilege of running away from parliament when they ought to be sitting here attending to public matters.

The reference made by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) with regard to members getting mileage does not apply to me. I think that every hon. member should get his actual travelling expenses. If he has to pay passage on a steamboat or even a railway, which does not give passes, he should be refunded the amount paid. As far as I am concerned, ever since I have been a member, I have only charged my actual expenses coining here, and I find from the reports I get. that there has only been one member of this House who ever did the same, and that is Lord Stratlicona, so that I am in Lord Strathcona's class.
The MINISTER OF ItAILW'YS AND CANALS. Does the hon. gentleman feel like forgiving Lord Stratlicona ?
I forgive any man who does right.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he sees any objection to including members of the provincial legislatures among those entitled to passes, because, as the Bill stands, we prevent passes being given to them. We should at least allow railway companies the option of giving passes to members of the local legislatures if they choose.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if the provision compelling : railway companies to carry members of

parliament free, compels these companies to carry them free all over the country. Why should we pass legislation compelling the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Grand Trunk Railway to carry a member of parliament, say from Kingston or Welland to the Pacific coast for nothing, when not engaged on parliamentary duties. It is all very well to compel a company to carry a member of parliament free to his parliamentary duties, but why should it be compelled to carry him all over the country on his own private business ? I may have private business in Abincouver or in any other part of the Dominion, and I fail to see why a railway company should be compelled to carry me free simply because I am a member of parliament. I think it well enough that there should be a clause providing that a railway company should be compelled to carry a member of parliament from his place of residence to the capital. Or, take It, as, for instance, with the Canadian Pacific Railway, which issues passes good for lines east of Port Arthur, or the Grand Trunk Railway, which issues passes for its lines in Canada. The Grand Trunk Railway has a line extending to Chicago. Surely, it should not be incumbent upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company to carry me or any other member of parliament to Chicago on my private affairs free of charge.
I think the suggestion is going too far, and it might very fairly be changed. I have no interest in railway companies, but I do not believe in stipulating that a railway company shall be under obligation to carry me over their whole system because I happen to be a member of parliament.
I have listened very carefully to the hou. member for Welland (Mr. German), and in reply I think a very apt quotation in his case would be : ' Me thinks the lady doth protest too much.'

There may be something in the contention of the hou. member for Welland (Mr. German). But it seems to me that, instead of the free use of their passes by members of parliament in travelling about the country being a matter of complaint, a great deal of the time of this House would be saved if hon. members would travel more, and so understand better the subjects that come up here for debate. Many of us are ignorant of large portions of the Dominion and its actual resources, and not in a position to discuss intelligently questions arising in connection with those localities. It is all very well to assume a high tone of morality and all that kind of thing, but let us get down to common sense. If we do, we shall use our passes and gain a greater knowledge of the affairs of the countrv. so as to be able to discuss to fetter advantage questions coming before the House.

If I were not a democrat, I would move that the railway eom-Mr. GERMAN. [DOT]
panies should be compelled to furnish members of parliament with private cars, but being a democrat, I do not do so. I am surprised, however, that hon. gentlemen should talk of members travelling on passes on their private business. The railway companies should provide passes, not only for members of parliament, but for members' wives also.
On section 205,

I move that this section be amended by striking out the words * in the case of a railway not subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, but ' and inserting the following : ' in the case of any railway, whether subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada or not.' I think that the substitution of these words is necessary to make it perfectly clear. And the principle it seems to me to be a sound one-that if a railway company, whether subject to the legislative authority of this parliament or not, receives a subsidy from this parliament in aid of its construction, the acceptance of that aid should be taken as a covenant with the Dominion of Canada that the erection of stations shall be under the control of the board. And I may say that I have embodied a clause to this effect in every contract that has been made within recent years, so that these railways are already bound. But it seems to me well to put it in the Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) will pardon me the suggestion that if the railway is not subject to our legislative authority, it must be subject to the authority of the province, and the question naturally arises whether a railway company subject to the legislative authority of the province can contract itself out of its obligation to be subject to the law of the province, and virtually make a contract to conform to the law of this parliament.
This clause would not prevent the provinces insisting upon stations being built under their direction.

Then, you would have this delightful condition-the province might say : You shall have a station at this point; while the federal authority would intervene and say : You shall fix a station for the same locality at this other point. So, the company would have two stations for the same locality.
It would cause inconvenience, but all I meant was that this would not prevent the province exercising its rights.

It is within the power of this parliament to make the enactment, I believe. These companies, as I have said, as

a condition of receiving subsidy from this parliament allow tbe government of the Dominion to indicate where the stations shall be built. That being a matter of contract, we only embodied a clause in this Bill to name the tribunal by whom that jurisdiction or authority of the Crown may be exercised, and we name the board as that authority. It does not affect the status of the road in any particular. The railway, company have power to make such a contract. They have received the consideration in respect of which it is made, and we only say that the board shall represent the Crown in the enforcement and carrying out of the contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Let me make myself clear. As between the railway company and the government, if the company have received a subsidy subject to this obligation, we can, by legislation, give legislative effect to that obligation. But that is not particularly what I wished to say. If the company is under the legislative control of the provincial legislature then the provincial legislation would apply with respect to the location of the line and the location of the stations. But if the company enter into a contract with the Dominion government, so far as the company itself is concerned, it would be binding on the company, but it cannot be binding upon the provincial legislature. So the result would be that you will have two authorities to consider. You have the provincial authority, which undoubtedly has a right to determine the location of the stations ; then you have the Dominion authority exercised by virtue of this con-tractural obligation with respect to the same subject matter. I submit this point to the Minister of Railways, though there may not be much in it.

I do not think any inconvenience is likely to result, because the provincial government may have given a subsidy and many have an interest in the railway. There will be nothing to prevent a railway company from entering into a binding contract with any provincial government or any private individual by which that government or individual will make a contribution ami give to the company some money or other consideration on condition that the company will contract to locate and maintain a station at some particular point on their line which may be named by the person who has contributed. In that case the contract can be enforced against the company and no question can arise. The company lias chosen to make such a contract, believing it would be more to its advantage to receive this subsidy encumbered with that condition attached to it than not to receive tin-subsidy and to be free from the condition. All we desire to do is to indicate that the board shall be the tribunal which shall execute the will, the declared intention and the purpose of the government in that regard.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It might be doubtful whether the board could enforce that decision. Supposing that the company might not like the decision and wanted to resort to every means it could to get out of complying with that decision, no doubt the case would ultimately have to go before a court. The provincial legislature, for instance, might have made an order to comply with the very subject matter that this board was trying to force compliance with. The board would say :	We want you to comply with
this matter in such and such a way. While the provincial legislature would say : You must comply with the matter in another way. Now that is a question affecting the same station, not two stations, one and the same question that both parties are dealing with. Now the legislature might say that was not a sufficient compliance with the contract, or the railway commissioners might say it was not sufficient in their opinion. In that case the question of jurisdiction would ultimately be forced into some court for decision. In any case which is sought to be covered by this section, it seems to me the court would be obliged to decide that thei provincial authority should govern, and that the order of our board would be nugatory.

Where a railway company makes a contract with the government which gives a subsidy of so much in aid of the construction of the railway on condition that the government name the places where the stations shall be located, that is wholly a matter of contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would you not have to have the provincial legislature agree to that ? They may have control of that railway.

I do not know whether the provincial government could make such conditions ; but supposing they did, we are not concerned about that. It is our business to see that they carry out their contract with us, and it is the business of the provincial government to see that they carry out their contract with them ; and if the provincial government have made an improvident contract is not our look-out. I do not think a conflict is likely to arise, even from a con-tractural point of view. I do not think the board would unreasonably insist upon a location which was satisfactory to every body else.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I wish to propose an amendment to the Bill, a notice of which lion, gentlemen may find in the Votes and Proceedings of Monday, 8th June.

Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.l. An amendment to what section ?

I will leave it to the minister to say to what section it should he added. The amendment is intended to compel railway companies in the prairie country to tire-guard their lines, and thus prevent the spread of prairie fires which, from year to year, have, since the opening of that country, done serious damage. Wo have discussed at great length in this House the cattle-guard question, which is recognized as of great importance to the agricultural community ; yet I venture to say that every year as much damage is done in the Northwest Territories by prairie fires breaking out along the lines of railway as is done in five years throughout the whole of Canada by reason of defective cattle-guards. Now the subject of this amendment was discussed at considerable length towards the end of last session, as lion, gentlemen will see who care to look up the second volume of ' Hansard,' page 4582. I trust it is not necessary for us at this time to go into the subject as exhaustively as we did then. The proposed amendment obtained last year a favourable reception by a considerable majority of the members of the House, but on account of the late date the matter came up, and upon the suggestion of the right lion, the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition, the amendment was withdrawn at that time. The amendment I propose now is the following :
1.	Every railway company owning or operating a railway in the North-west Territories shall, on or before the 31st day of July in each year, provide a fireguard on each side of the line of railway upon any uncultivated or unoccupied land not covered by timber adjoining such railway, consisting of a strip of ploughed land at least eight feet in width which shall at all times thereafter during the year be kept free from grass and other inflammable matter.
(2.) The fireguard shall be distant at least three hundred feet from the centre line of the railway, and the company shall cause the grass to be burned off between it and such centre line not later than the 1st day of August in each year.
(3.) The company shall, when causing such grass to be burned, have present sufficient persons and appliances to prevent the fire from spreading.
2.	Any company neglecting or failing to comply with any of the provisions of the foregoing seotion, and the officers and directors thereof, shall be liable, on summary conviction, to a penalty of $1,000 for each day of such neglect.
3.	For the purpose of complying with the provisions of section one hereof the company may enter upon any land not owned by it, and no claim for damages .shall be maintained against the company for any act done in compliance with the provisions of the said section one.
This amendment follows in principle the legislation that has been adopted in the North-west legislature on the subject of prairie fires, so far as that legislature has Mr. SCOTT.
jurisdiction ; that is to say that every individual and company, in that part of the country, which is subject to the jurisdiction of the legislature, is obliged, when using fire in any way, to take precautions against the spread of the fire. This is such a serious matter out there that the ordinary provisions throwing the liability upon parties for damage from fire are not deemed sufficient, and specific safeguards are provided which every person must use or be liable to punishment for failure to do so.
Why does the hon. gentleman confine this amendment to the North-west Territories ?

The amendment only covers the North-west Territories. I think it will only be found feasible to apply it iu a part of the country where the settlement is very sparse. It will not be feasible where there is any considerable settlement and where the land is cultivated alongside the railway. The North-west Territories comprise practically all of what is known as the semi-arid country, the purely ranching country and that is the only part of the country where probably provisions such as these are practicable.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word in corroboration of the remarks of the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) as I did when he brought the subject before the House at the last session of parliament. I do not think that the hon. members from the eastern provinces can realize the 'enormous extent of the damage which has been done in that particular section of the country which he represents by fires arising from sparks spreading from railway engines The fires have in many cases been of an extremely destructive character, not only in so far as the private property of individuals has been concerned, but the damage has been of such a character at times that immense grazing areas upon which large herds of cattle have depended have been entirely destroyed. So that, not only has there been private damage but there has been damage to the community. My own recollection of the law in the province of Manitoba on the subject of fires- I speak subject to correction as I have not looked into it for some time-is that practically it amounts to this that any person who kindles a fire or allows it to spread is liable not only to an action for civil damages, but he is also liable to a fine and to a heavy penalty. What has always struck me as being a most remarkable and indefensible anomaly in our law is that the one institution which is most likely to set fire and which, as a matter of fact, does most of the damage, should practically be put in such a position that it is impossible that any penalty could be applied and it was practically impossible that damages

could be recovered. The lawyers in the House are familiar with the fact that when an action) for damages is brought it is necessary to show there has been negligence, and if that cannot be shown substantively, if it cannot be shown that the railway company did not have the latest and best appliances for preventing sparks from spreading! from the engine the complainant fails. As a matter of fact, lawyers all know that it is, in the great majority of cases, quit*? impossible to prove any such thing, and in four cases out of five when an aggrieved person goes to a lawyer for the purpose of getting advice, he is advised that he will save time and money by not bringing any action. I have known in my own constituency of most grievous cases in which the entire property of individuals has been destroyed by fires set out by sparks from engines. It might appear to be a hardship to some extent that railway companies should be obliged to pay damages in all cases, but I am prepared to say, speaking for myself, that I think they ought to be liable for damages resulting from fires in any event. But, the hon. member for West As'siniboia does not, in his amendment, ask to go so far. He simply asks that the House should say that if the circumstances are such that by a small expenditure of money the setting out of fires can be prevented the railway company ought to be compelled to do that. It seems to me that proposition ought to meet with the approval of the members of the House without exception. I suggested to my hon. friend a moment ago, when he mentioned the amendment to me, that there were places where in all probability the amendment which he suggests would not apply. He has referred to the fact that in thickly settled districts where the farms are alongside the railway, and are occupied, it would be impossible to carry out the provisions of this amendment. Some other provision would have to be devised for such cases, but there are great stretches of country where this provision might be applied without practically any difficulty and at a comparatively small expense. It seems to me that in such a case the House ought to require that it should be applied. I suggested to my hon. friend that the question as to where fireguards should be required should be placed within some such authority as the railway commission which ought to be placed in a position to decide that point so that the railway company; would not be put to unnecessary expense and it would see that the intention of the amendment was carried out.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to detain the House for a moment, but I simply rise to express my appreciation of the amendment which has been submitted for your consideration. As I represent a prairie riding and four railways will be passing through the entire length of my
constituency, and as I have had considerable experience in cases such as the hon. minister-

speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill (No. 209) respecting certain aid for the extension of the Canadian Northern Railway Company.-The Minister of Railways.
On section 6-control of tolls on all lines of company,
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS [DOT] CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair). I propose to ask the committee to add to section 6 the following words :
Provided that the rates or tolls to be charged shall not in any case be higher than the rates or tolls which may be fixed in the contract to be made between the government of Canada and the Canadian Northern Railway Company under this Act.
I do not under-tands that clause. Does it enable you to fix any rate you choose, and that the board of commissioners shall not have any control over it ?
The board of railway commissioners will not be able to make the rates any higher. After they are fixed by contract with the government the board will not be empowered to make them any higher.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I presume this clause is introduced in accordance with the suggestions made at an earlier stage in regard to maximum rates. May I ask what kind of goods these rates will be fixed for ?

There will be certain general commodities that undoubtedly the contract will make provision for-grain, lumber, mill stuffs and coal. We can name these four at present, but there may be something in addition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can you give the House any idea of what you propose to do in this contract which you intend to enter into ?

We propose to have the tariff placed on as low a basis as we feel we can properly place it, having regard to other roads and the tolls that are imposed. I cannot -enter into the matter with more
,5787

particularity at the present moment. We had some suggestions from the gentlemen who represent the district through which this road will run and our intention is to provide for the covering of these four specific classes of goods. I would not limit ourselves as to that, but we are prepared to go that far as to these four. I could not indicate the precise tariff at the present moment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In a large portion of the country through which this railway would be built there is an established rate on other railways at the present time. Do you intend to take these rates as the maximum ?
Oh, yes; we do not propose to allow anything higher than the rates that exist,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you propose to cut the rates very much below these ? Have you formed any opinion upon that point, because it is rather important. You see, you are going into that district from which the Canadian Pacific Railway is now carrying grain. If you propose to take ten per cent or twenty per cent off these rates that will immediately affect the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. If you say that you will take the Canadian Pacific Railway rates as the maximum we will know somewhat what the government proposes. I should think the government would not enter into a contract by which the Canadian Northern Railway should be allowed higher rates than those existing ; but if the government stipulates that this company must have lower rates than are now asked by the other companies, that would mean of course a reduction by those other companies at once. I presume the government would not have decided upon such course without very careful consideration, and I think they should be prepared to tell the House now what the result of that consideration is.

I cannot do that. It would be quite impossible for us without proper consideration to determine what these rates will be. In a general way, I can, I think, state with confidence that we would not propose to allow any higher rates than the rates which now obtain. As to whether it would be found impossible to establish any lower, or much lower rates, I cannot say at the moment. I should think myself- of course it is for the government to determine and I can only speak my own mind on the subject-my own impression would be that we would rather recognize the zone basis for the different distances of say 100 miles each, perhaps more, perhaps less. The rate should be at such a figure and so on covering the entire territory which this road traverses up. to Edmonton. As to whether there would be any reduction below the ex-Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
isting rates is a matter which must be gone into very carefully and can only be decided upon after mature consideration, and no one in the government has as yet been able to address himself to the matter sufficiently to enable him or them to make a statement oil the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Let me see if I understand clearly what the effect of this .clause is. The government intend to make a rate with the Canadian Northern Railway on these four items, and that rate can in no case be exceeded by the railway commission, but they may fix lower rates.
We have discretion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is a rate agreed on at present between the Manitoba government and the Canadian Northern Railway as to the carrying of grain from Winnipeg and points in Manitoba. The rates fixed by this government will not be higher than these rates at present agreed upon between the Manitoba government and the Canadian Northern Railway. Am I right ?

I think probably that the hon. gentleman is as nearly correct as one can be. The territory to which these rates will apply will be territory outside of the limit covered by any existing arrangement between the Canadian Northern Railway and the Manitoba government. There would no doubt be a disposition on the part of the government in settling a rate, to be guided very much by the existing arrangement as far as it will apply, and to make it applicable as much as possible to the territory beyond.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It will work out in rather a curious way when you come to fix through-rates. You will have a portion of this system which will be controlled by the government of Manitoba in their agreement confirmed by the legislature of Manitoba and further confirmed by this parliament, over which the government of Manitoba has power to fix rates over a line which may be a portion of this general system. How will that work out in the result V You will have that authority acknowledged by this parliament as an authority having power to control the rates and that will extend over a portion of the line. Then you will have the authority designated by this parliament in the proposed board of railway commissioners which, within certain limits fixed by the contract referred to, will have the power to control the rates over the system beyond the confines of Manitoba. I do not myself see very clearly just how that is going to work out in the result. I have no doubt the minister has given consideration to it, and perhaps he will be good enough to say a few words in regard

to the matter, so that we may clearly understand.

I do not see any difficulty In the working of it at all. So far as the control of the rates is concerned-I am using the word ' control ' in its widest signification- the control rests in the government of Canada and would rest in any tribunal which the parliament of Canada would constitute for the purpose. While there may be contractual arrangements between the government of Manitoba and the Canadian Northern Railway, which would be enforcible I presume as against the Canadian Northern Railway by that government, it is only because they have made a contract and not because of legislation which they may themselves have passed, that they have what they call a control. All the same, the government of Canada could allow higher rates or could reduce them to a lower figure, and so far as this allowance of the larger rates is concerned it would be only subject to the restrictions which this Act imposes, and the discretion of the commission which is given under the Bill. The fact of the government of Manitoba having an arrangement in their territory, must enter very largely, and no doubt will enter very largely, into the determination as to what would be the rate which would govern beyond. That is not because the government has made any arrangement with the Canadian Northern Railway, but because the Canadian Northern Railway are bound to make certain rates over a portion of their territory. As certain rates are fixed on a part of their line, I apprehend that the government will feel at liberty to enforce a particular rate on the part which is outside and beyond Manitoba. In the practical working out there will be no inconvenience or difficulty. We prepare a schedule for the different distances. They are all through-rates very largely, as far as these particular articles are concerned, and not purely local rates, for small distances. What the people are most interested in is the long haul.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not quite agree with the hon. minister as to one view he expresses. Speaking off-hand and without precise recollection of the terms of the contract between Manitoba and the Canadian Northern, I would think that this government might fix a lower rate within the province of Manitoba than that which has been fixed by the Manitoba government. But this government could not, without practically repealing the statute of 1901, which confirmed the contract between Manitoba and the Canadian Northern-and to do so would be a breach of faith-legalize within the province of Manitoba higher rates. I dare say that this government, in virtue of the power it can exercise over railways. might fix a lower rate, but I do not
think, as against the government and people of Manitoba, that it could fairly fix a higher rate and authorize the company to charge that rate, because to do that would be to repeal the statute we have already passed confirming the bargain between the Canadian government and the government of Manitoba. When you come to fix through-rates, are they not fixed over a long haul, say from Edmonton to the Atlantic ? Would they not be supposed to be fixed on a somewhat different basis than over a shorter haul.
A lesser rate per mile.

Then you see that the rate fixed by the government of Manitoba, within its own boundary, might not be of much assistance when fixing a through-rate from Edmonton. Here you have a Bill giving you power to fix through-rates over the entire system, and you have a portion of that system controlled by this parliament and another portion controlled by the Manitoba legislature. With these divided authorities, how are you to control the rates ? Suppose you desire to fix through-rates from Edmonton to Fort William ; over a portion of that line the legislature of Manitoba has the power to fix the minimum rate and over the rest of the system, from the confines of Manitoba westward, you have the railway commission controlling the rates, subject to the limitation fixed by this statute ; how is that to work out practically ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. It must be borne in mind that the powers given the province of Manitoba to fix the rates are not confined within the limits of the province, but extend from its western limit down to Lake Superior, in the province of Ontario; and as my hon. leader has just said, it would be a bad feature if this Bill would interfere with the powers of the local legislature by giving power to the railway commission to increase the rates which might be fixed by Manitoba. In that contract with the Canadian Northern, the province of Manitoba assumed a very large responsibility. If the road is not a paying institution, the province becomes liable for the interest on the bonds which it has guaranteed, and as this power to fix the rates has not been given without consideration, I think we should look twice before we interfere with it.

We are not interfering with the legislature of Manitoba in the slightest degree. The hon. gentleman will admit that this Bill recognizes and declares that the existing rates shall not be increased.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. What will happen if the province of Manitoba should think proper to lower the rates ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the rates should be lowered, that would be certainly a matter which the Governor in Council would have to consider when fixing a schedule, under this contract to be entered into with the Canadian Northern. I am unable to see the difficulty or trouble which my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) anticipates. I do not see how it could possibly arise. The further west you go, the longer the haul to Lake Superior; and the necessary result would be that in fixing the rates from the western boundary of Manitoba to Lake Superior, any change must be in the way of reduction. When you double the distance of the haul you reduce the rate per mile.
speakername: Tlie MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Supposing you choose to fix rates on traffic passing through the province of Manitoba higher than the province of Manitoba contracted for ? I presume that, under this Bill, this company would have authority to do that. Otherwise the Act would have no force.
It is the other way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would it not be necessary to make this Bill subject to any contract this company has lawfully entered into ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the province of Manitoba has the right to define what the rates shall be in its territory and the board has the right to fix a higher rate, for this company, the question will be which is to govern ?

It seems to me that the very reverse would be likely to follow. I do not want to enter into any discussion as to the ethics of the question, but I am under the impression that what legislation was passed by this parliament in respect of that contract was only of a confirmatory character. All that parliament did was to say in effect that the legislature of Manitoba had full power to enact the contract as it did. We did not commit ourselves as a parliament to the adoption of that contract. We did not appropriate the contract to ourselves. All we said was that it is a legal contract, so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned. It did not curtail In the slightest degree the power of this parliament to control rates in that country-not in the legislative point of view. That is the view I take. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

The hon. gentleman has not answered my question. He knows there is all the difference in the world between the two conditions. We annex,this amendment to this clause for what reason ? The object that every government has in view in taking any authority over the rates of a railway, is to keep them down. There is no danger of any quarrel

to get them up. So no practical question arises. by these rates, because yon have yourselves declaimed that you will be prepared to carry traffic at these rates, and youi cannot complain if we fix them. in that event I am under an entire misapprehension. ment was not in that debate controverted but was accepted by the House without dispute, that we acted at that time upon this assumption, that we had that understanding at that time and no attempt to dispute it or in any way detract from the force of that position being taken has occurred either on the part of the federal authority or on the part of the provincial authority. next year.
