The remarks of the leader of the opposition indicated, that I quoted the statement of the Attorney General of the province of Manitoba as indicating what is the effect of the legislation passed by this House. I presume that it will be unnecessary for me to explain that I had no intention of suggesting any such meaning. The quotation which I made in that connection, was for the purpose of showing that there was not any misunderstanding on the part of the members of the Manitoba government in regard to the effect of our legislation ; but, that when the Act was passed by this House it was with the full understanding of the legal effect which I maintained to be perfectly clear and unimpaired, namely, that we retain the right to fix the maximum rate and that we did not impair our power in anyway whatever by passing that legislation.
The gentlemen on the other side of the House admitted it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It seems to me that there is more consideration given to this question of rates now than was given to it at the time the Manitoba Bill was passed. It is my recollection that when the Manitoba legislation first came up in the local House, it was discovered that they, the company, required auxiliary or enabling legislation to enable them to make such a bargain with the government of Manitoba. The question of rates was not at all under consideration, and it did not assume that phase until it came down here. The speech which was then made Mr. Campbell, the Attorney General of Manitoba, and part of which was read by the Minister of the Interior to-night, was made more for political purposes than as dealing practically with the Bill. If we wish to quote some of the utterances that were made on this Bill, I think we might take those of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who is one of the oldest parliamentarians here, a gentleman who has a good deal of experience in matters of this sort. After quoting from the speech of the Attorney General Campbell, he said
That is the statement of Mr. Campbell, and it will be observed that he states plainly that the Dominion government may fix maximum rates But he does not state that the Dominion government may increase the rates, that it may override the action of Manitoba in any direction or in a,ny manner that it may deem advisable in the public interest , and he does not state that the putting of rates below a reasonable figure, while it would benefit the people of Manitoba so far as freight rates are concerned, would leave tne * people of Manitoba to pay the deficiency

which was caused by putting rates below a proper figure.
Again :
And he does not say to the people of Manitoba that these rates that he is talking about, which the Dominion government may revise, which the Dominion government may increase, and which, if lower than a paying rate the government of Manitoba must make up indirectly'if not directly-he does not say that these rates are, in any event probably higher than the actual natural rates charged for business will be within two or three years, when other railway lines are completed, and when Manitoba is enjoying the benefits of competition that will come without guarantee, without liability, without incurring the obligations he would recommend. Again :
Yet in return for that obligation she was getting absolute control of rates, when the truth is that she has not such control, the Dominion having paramount authority, the railway committee of the Privy Council can treat these rates in any manner it chooses-if the public interests require it the rates can be raised as well as lowered.
Here is the point I want bon. gentlemen to observe.
The interests of Ontario against discriminating rates can be protected by raising them.
The point was then taken that the province of Manitoba had not the power to revise the rates in the province of Ontario, and lion, members opposite will not contend that it has. A portion of this system runs beyond Manitoba. The hon. member for Provencber (Mr. LaRiviere) has said that the province of Manitoba had control of the rates from Winnipeg to Fort William The idea is preposterous. The Dominion goi eminent can raise or lower the rates between Fort William and Winnipeg. Suppose there should be a failure of crops for two years in Manitoba, and that province would have to pay this $673,000 annual interest due. This road would not be able to pay that interest, and the province would have to do so. And suppose the railway promoters stood in with the provincial government and said : Do not lower those rates, let the debt accumulate on the province. In such an event, the government of the Dominion might possibly have to come to the assistance of the province to help it out of its difficulties. It would never do lor this governmont to divest itself of control over the rates, either bv lowering or raising them. The full power of controlling these rates is just as much with the Dominion government now as when the Manitoba bargain with the Canadian Northern Railway was passed.

If this section should Pass. as It stands, it will put it within the province of the Railway Commission to render absolutely nugatory the agreement entered into between the Manitoba government and the Canadian Northern Railway. Mr. McCreary.
That contract gave the control of the rates to the Manitoba government.
You are speaking of the original section without the amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
1 do not intend to enter into any discussion concerning the agreement between the Canadian Northern Railway and the province of Manitoba, nor do I intend to discuss the question as to what legal power the province of Manitoba has, under its agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway, to fix rates ; but as this discussion touches the question as to whether the province of Manitoba has any power under that agreement to regulate the rates, it seems to me that there should be a rider added to this section No. 6. I have drafted a very short one, to which I would ask the consideration of the hon. the Minister of Railways. I would propose to add these words :
Subject, however, to any rights which the province of Manitoba may haVe, under its agreement with the Canadian Northern, to fix rates.
There is nothing in that rider which admits that the province of Manitoba has jurisdiction to fix the rates ; but if it has, then there would be nothing in this Bill which would prejudice that right. I merely throw this out as a suggestion.

I can see very serious objection to adding those words. I venture to say that there is not any gentleman learned in the law in this House who will express the opinion that the Dominion parliament has divested itself of the entire and absolute control over the rates on railways through Manitoba and any portion 'of the territory that the Manitoba agreement may effect. There was no lawyer of any standing who expressed that opinion when the Manitoba contract and legislation were under consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why were not those clauses in that Bill struck out ? Why were they left there ? And why did this parliament ratify and confirm that agreement ? It is only under that agreement that any question can be raised as to the power of Manitoba to fix the rates.

There could be no question in my mind. I have not heard yet any lawyer of standing express the opinion that our legislation in respect of Manitoba robs us of any portion of our power or control over the rates. All we did was, as far as our legislative sanction went, to legalize the legislation which had been passed by the Manitoba government, a portion of which was clearly passed by a body incompetent to legislate fully and properly in that direction. They came to us and said : We have asked the Canadian Northern Railway to make an agreement with us to allow us, as between ourselves and them, to control the rates-not as between the Crown, as represented by the government of Canada and the Canadian Northern Railway, but as between the Canadian Northern Railway and the Manitoba government. We said :	Go
ahead. We will say, if you wish, that you had power to make such a contract; but we did not thereby divest ourselves of the legislative power that resides, and resides only, in the parliament of this Dominion. The ex-Minister of Railways did not hesitate to declare that we were not giving away our legislative power, that we were not surrendering any power, and other hon. gentlemen affirmed the same thing. That Act passed with the fullest knowledge that we were just as free to pass any legislation we might deem proper regarding the control of rates in that territory as if the Manitoba Bill had never become law. But my hon. friend (Mr. Pringle) asks us to add words to this clause which would recognize that the province of Manitoba and the entire district that comes within the operation of that contract are withdrawn from the control of this parliament. He is asking us to surrender our control and to say that neither the Railway Board nor any other tribunal we may establish is competent to deal with this question and that, therefore, we will
hand it over to the Manitoba government. He asks us to add these words : ' subject, however, to any rights which the province of Manitoba may have, under its agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway, to fix rates.' Of course, my hon. friend might say, if they have not the power, this does not give them any. But is it not the legislative recognition of a doubt at least ? Is it not tantamount to a parliamentary declaration that we believe they have such control . under the legislation we passed a while ago, and, therefore, we must re-affirm our own power ? I could not accept this amendment for that reason. I can not, for the life of me, understand what this discussion means. I cannot see the point or relevance of it. There is no question but that the power of the parliament of Canada is today as full and ample as ever it was. Then what reason is there for us to say that we ought to denude ourselves of it either in whole or in part ? As to this discussion having a practical effect, I fail to discover a trace of it. Every body knows that the only question that can arise is with reference not to raising but to lowering the rates, and the whole effort of the people is not to get the rates up but to get them down. And when parliament says that no commission which may be constituted, or the Governor in Council, when it comes to deal with this question, its efforts will not be to get the rates up, but to reduce the rates. Now the third clause of the Act passed by the parliament of Canada which we have been discussing provides that nothing in (his Act or in the indentures or schedules made in pursuance of it shall limit the rights and powers existing in the parliament of Canada, the Governor in Council, the Railway Committee of the Privy Council or other commission or authority. 'Does not that settle it, if there was any question about it before ? Then what is it we are debating ? Why it is not even an academic question, for my hon. friend himself will not say that there is any doubt in his mind as to the full power of this parliament to legislate as it pleases. He has not said that and he will not say it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I have said exactly the contrary over and over again.

Then if he has stated the contrary, what is the point in the suggestion that there will be some conflict ? There will be no conflict if we have supreme powers. In working out all these things there may be difficulties, but it is tiio business of those working them to overcome those difficulties. We do not wish to get into unpleasant conflict with the government of Manitoba, nor would any commission wish to do so. But their effort will be to get the rates down. That is what the people want, and the commission will not wish to antagonize pub-

Ho opinion, nor will the Governor in Council. Wlvat, then, is the use of talking about the question when we are all agreed ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister has said that I stated that the Bill passed by this parliament with reference to the contract made by the Manitoba government did not abrogate our power. Every one agrees to that. We have full power to abrogate any contract we enter into without compensation to the individual.
Does the hon. gentleman say that we entered into a contract ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I say we entered into a contract. Why what are the facts ? The two parties come here to get the provincial legislation confirmed, for they had not the power to confirm it themselves, there being a reserve power in the Dominion government. We are the empowering party. To the extent that we ratify that legislation, we are a consenting party.
We did it with all sorts of reservations.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. minister is too good a lawyer not to know that that is mere surplusage. We had all these powers without reserving them in an Act of parliament. In this respect we are in the same position as we are in with regard to a contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other company. We have the power to break any of those contracts tomorrow without indemnifying the parties concerned to the extent of one cent. There is no one who doubts our power. But what we argue is that, having, as empowering party, given our authority to this contract, we are bound by the contract and are bound not to interfere with it in any manner without sufficient reason and without indemnity. That is all we maintain. The hon. minister asks what we are fighting about. The hon. minister loftily looks at members on this side as though to say : You poor fools, you have been talking for a long time, but you do not know what you are talking about. Why, suppose the commission fixed a rate of twenty-five cents for carrying grain in Manitoba, while the bargain between Manitoba and the Canadian Northern Railway called fqj a rate of twenty cents. The superior power is with the Dominion government to fix the rates. What then would he the effect, but to abrogate the contract between the Manitoba government and the company to that extent. All we ask of the minister is that the rate fixed in the schedule shall not be higher than the present rate charged in Manitoba by the agreement between the Manitoba government and llie Canadian Northern Railway. He refuses to consent to that.
Hon. Mr, BLAIR.
I did not refuse to consent to it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He refuses to consent to anything. He reserves to himself the power to put in the schedule rates which will give the Canadian Northern Railway a different bargain from the one they have with the Manitoba government.
Why not ?
Because it is bad faith. We empowered the Manitoba government to enter into that contract with the Canadian Northern Railway by confirming the agreement. And now, we break the agreement.
This Bill does not interfere with the Manitoba arrangement.

The hon. member (Mr. Scott) seems to differ in his interpretation of the clause from all the rest of the House. The hon. minister told us a little while ago that they have the fixing of the rates in the North-west and from Manitoba to Lake Superior, and lie might have gone further, and said that under this clause he has the fixing of the rates in Manitoba itself. The hon. minister will not deny it.
That is not being granted by this Bill. It exists. It is set forth in the Railway Commission Bill and is already the law.
Then, what does the hon. member (Mr. Scott) say to the contract we empowered the government of Manitoba to make with the Canadian Northern Railway ?
My contention is that this Bill does not interfere with it any more than it has been interfered with by Dominion legislation for the last two years.

Dominion legislation does not interfere with it. But under this Bill the hon. minister takes the power specifically to fix the schedule rates. It was never interfered with before. He takes the power under this Bill to fix the prices they shall charge.
Not on traffic originating in Manitoba or destined to points in Manitoba, but only originating on or destined to points on the line we are now aiding which is nearly all outside of Manitoba.

Further, 1 have put forward the argument that, with regard to certain railroads under provincial jurisdiction, in Manitoba, I doubt whether the Commission Bill would apply. The hon. minister says it applies to all railways. He says, further, that when the commission fix rates, the railway companies cannot charge less.
That is not new law.
It is new law ; it never was in force before.
The power has always existed. We are simply creating a new tribunal to exercise that power.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that it never was law before.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) is right. It was always the law. May I ask the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) a question ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well ?
Will the hon. gentleman say that, in this clause or any portion of it, the government is asking parliament to give it any more power than it would have if the clause were not in the Bill ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will tell the hon. minister what might be urged very well with regard to that. There is a principle well known to the hon. minister, but, perhaps not so well known to my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver), or to my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. 'Scott). It is that a general statute does not ordinarily repeal a. special statute. You may very well! argue that the provisions of the general statute would not interfere with the Act of two years ago. But in dealing in this special Act with the same railway, section 6 might have an operation by way of repealing that Act which the general statute would not have.

Does my hon. friend say that the legislation which was passed in connection with the Manitoba Bill, took away or diminished in any particular the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada to control rates ?	*
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I told my hon. friend over and over again that so far as the technical power is concerned it certainly does not ; neither does the passing of this Act take away our power, the technical power of parliament, hereafter to modify any of its provisions. The passing by this parliament of an enactment that the lands of the Canadian Pacific Railway should not be taxed until after a certain period, did not take away from parliament the technical pdwer to repeal that provision the next year if it wished. Every one understands that, it is not necessary for the hon. gentleman to emphasize that, we have not denied it, we have affirmed it over and over again.

Does the hon. gentleman say that by enabling the Canadian Northern to make a contract with the Manitoba government so that it would be legal as between the two parties, we thereby deprived ourselves or surrendered tbe general control of parliament over the rates on that line that we formerly possessed ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If I have not made my position clear, I fear it is hopeless to attempt to do so any further. It is the case of any two parties who required a contract to be confirmed and who come to this parliament to have it confirmed. Parliament has the right to repeal such a statute or to modify it in any way it sees fit ; but it does not usually do so without having the consent of the parties.

We simply state to the Canadian Northern Railway and to the province of Manitoba : We will allow you to make this contract between yourselves, and since you cannot make it without our coming to your assistance, we will give you the authority to make it. But we do not divest ourselves or limit ourselves temporarily or otherwise in respect of the rights which we possess as a parliament over the whole subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would have no objection to adding to the clause something like this :
' Provided, however, that nothing herein contained shall repeal, modify or affect the provisions of the Act, 1, Edw. vii, chapter 52, entitled an Act respecting the Canadian Northern Railway.' Then you are making it clear that you are not by this statute repealing the statute of two years ago or modifying it. That is not open to the objection' the hon. gentleman raised to the proposed amendment of my hon. friend from Cornwall. Now, with regard to the observations of my hon. friends from the North-west Territories with respect to any remarks that I have made, I have no doubt that they did not intentionally misconstrue them ; but I must insist that I shall be bound by what
1	have said with regard to this matter rather than by any construction which they have seen fit to place upon my remarks, which was not in accordance with my intention. I should unhesitatingly regard any observations I have made as tending to the advantage of the people of the Nortli-west Territories.

So far as the statute is concerned, it was very clear under section '
2	that the Canadian Northern Railway Company were given pretty full powers. Among those powers was the power of entering into this contract with the province of Manitoba. Now with regard to the contract itself, the whole gist of it is that in consideration of the guarantee of the said bonds the assignment of the said lines, &e., the Lieutenant Governor in Council shall from time to time fix the rates to be charged or demanded by the company. Now I apprehend there is no question that the Canadian Northern Railway would be bound by their contract, it having been declared in this Act that they had full power to enter into

that contract with the province of Manitoba, and the whole gist of this contract being the guarantee of these bonds, the consideration being that the Lieutenant Governor in Council of Manitoba had power to fix the rates. Now if the Lieutenant Governor in Council of Manitoba fixes the rates with the Canadian Northern Railway, I understand the minister's contention is that while it might be binding on the Canadian Northern, it is not in any way binding on the Dominion of Canada, that is, the Dominion of Canada can override anything that is done by the province of Manitoba. But would it be fair, when the province of Manitoba guaranteed these bonds on the sole consideration that they would have the power to fix these rates, that this parliament should override these rates so long as they are fair and equitable ? Now the clause I proposed to add did not in any way commit this parliament to the position of taking away from the Manitoba government the power to fix these rates. I was very careful in my language not to put it in that form. I simply said :
Subject, however, to any rights which the province of Manitoba may have under their agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway.
Now it seems to me it is only reasonable that that language should be added to that clause. But I do not apprehend that this Bill, so long as the rates were reasonable, would in any way interfere with the agreement made by the province of Manitoba with the Canadian Northern Railway.

I do not think that either the amendment moved by the member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) or that moved by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Borden) ought to be adopted. They are both very objectionable. The argument of the member for Cornwall, it seems to me, is one that bears strongly against his own proposition. He claims that the government of Manitoba were authorized by that Act to fix the rates upon the Canadian Northern within their territory. Now what does that expression mean ? It means that they are authorized by this parliament to make these rates as high or reduce them as low as they please. Now stop and consider, this is not a thing from which you can logically escape. Does the hon. member seriously think that, from any moral point of view, from any ethical point of view, from any view that ought to affect the conscience of parliament in trying to do what is just by the province of Manitoba, that we should hand over to the province of Manitoba the right to make the rates in that territory as high or as low as they please V They have great interest in making the rates high because they had assumed large obligations. They had undertaken to pay a tremendous amount of money every year, 5000,000 or $700,000 a year in the event of Mr. PRINGLE.
default by the company, a small province, with a small revenue and a large obligation. Now if we had power to cut the rates down but did not have any power to put them up, my hon. friend would be the first to argue that in cutting down the rates we are taking away the only security the government of Manitoba had to guarantee the repayment of their loan and to relieve themselves from their indemnity. Now can it be seriously argued in this House that we must stand with our hands tied helpless while the government of Manitoba are making the railway traffic pay just as large a figure as they choose ? My hon. friend made use of the words ' just and fair.' Who shall determine what is just and fair ? If his argument holds good, in ratifying this legislation we ought to say : We will allow you to exercise this power if you do it fairly and justly. It is too late for us to say that we ought now' to step in and revise or repeal or modify our legislation. We are not doing that, we are proposing to occupy the ground we have always occupied. By this Bill we take nothing away from Manitoba that w'e gave them, and we are not assuming any more authority than we have ever had since the Manitoba Bill was sanctioned by this parliament. It did not need any more legislation to say what the rates should be upon that line, even though these rates did not conform to the rates which the Manitoba government and the Canadian Northern had agreed upon. I must ask the committee not to accept either of these amendments. We ought not to recognize the surrender of w-hat we know we have never surrendered. We ought not to make any qualification which involves the suggestion that w'e have surrendered that jurisdiction either in law, equity or from any other point of view'.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister says that w-e have never surrendered that either in law, equity or from any other point of view.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If we had the power to prevent that bargain being made and after looking into the merits of the bargain and concluding it was one that ought to have been made, and after giving our sanction to the bargain, does the hon. minister think that we would be justified in doing something that would contradict the bargain that we sanctioned ?

I say unhesitatingly that we have not abandoned anything. We gave nothing in anyway, no pledge or guarantee, nor did w'e commit ourselves to the merits of the Bill in the slightest particular. So far as I am concerned I voted for the Bill, not because I believed in the merits of it; I-thought it was a very onerous undertaking

for the province of Manitoba to assume, but they could not legally execute it because the railway with which they were contracting Was a railway outside of the jurisdiction of the legislature of Manitoba, and therefore they could not make a contract with it. But I did not feel that this parliament should stand off and say :	We are better able to
judge as to whether you should enter into this contract or not. We will use the power we happen to possess and we will decline our aid in ratifying the contract you desire to enter into and would have entered into without any arrangement with us if it had not been that the railway company was a creature of this parliament. That was the sole reason. If you look at this Bill you will see, as I read it at all events, that parliament took the utmost pains to say that it was not giving up anything in conscience or in law in the way of power or authority or jurisdiction. It was just as free after this Bill was passed as before. We could repeal. I suppose, this legislation, although it is in the nature of a contract between parties, but I do not think we ought to repeal it. Then we would be open to the charge of having gone back upon an engagement we had entered into. But we retained all our powers unreservedly and without qualification when wre introduced this clause.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If there is no intention to repeal what is the objection to the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) V
Because, it is altogether unnecessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It may be unnecessary in one view but if we agree that there is no intention to repeal that is all the amendment of my hon. friend provides for.

My objection to it is that it may be said that parliament, in putting in that amendment, entertains doubts and that we were reiterating our authority. That would be putting parliament in a false position. We entertain no doubts because we have no doubt whatever that we have the power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it seems a very peculiar position for the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to take. He tells us that there was no merit whatever in this agreement, that the agreement was one by which the province of Manitoba might involve itself in an extraordinary liability and in great danger, that he saw nothing whatever in that agreement that was meritorious-
I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: A portion of the road that the Manitoba government is supposed to exercise control of 'lies outside the province of Manitoba and is in the province of Ontario. Supposing that the Manitoba government, having, according to the statements that these hon. gentlemen have made here, the right of raising the rates as well as lowering them, undertook to raise the rates in Ontario, where would the people of that portion of Ontario go to get relief ? Where would they be represented ? The hon. gentleman's argument is ridiculous.
They cannot have the power to reduce the rates unless they have the power to make them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) has asked a question as to a matter which is not in this discussion at all.
It is in this discussion.

It is not. In so far as I am concerned, I said that I was not discussing the legal aspect of the matter. The absolute power of controlling rates still remains with the Governor in Council and this parliament.

This railway, when it is constructed, will run from Edmonton to the lakes. A portion of it lies in the North-

west Territories and a portion in the province of Manitoba. If the hon. gentleman could have his ideas carried out there would be one rate existing in Manitoba which might be a great deal higher rate than that in the North-west Territories. How are you going to arrange that ? Are you going to have a division of authority as to railway rates all over the Dominion ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) was present during the full discussion of the Bill confirming this agreement between the province of Manitoba and the Canadian Northern Railway Company. He is perfectly well aware that the consideration of this contract was that the province of Manitoba should be able to enter into an agreement with the Canadian Northern Railway Company for the fixing of rates. I admit that it was understood in the discussion that the rates should be still subject to the control of the government in clause, but he supported this Bill and this very contract. The province of Manitoba has given a very valuable consideration to the Canadian Northern Railway Company for what ? Simply for the concession that the government of Manitoba could arrange the rates as between the Canadian Northern Railway and the province of Manitoba, subject, if you will, to the higher jurisdiction of the Governor in Council here. But, what I say here, as opposed to the statement made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, is that there certainly is a moral obligation upon this parliament to support any arrangement that is made by the province of Manitoba with the Canadian Northern Railway Company under this agreement, and it is ridiculous for the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to take the position that there are no merits in this agreement.
I did not say that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And that although it was dangerous to the province of Manitoba he voted for it.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if, when the government of Manitoba made this bargain, they had not their eyes open ? They knew that any rate they made would be subject to the control of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if when parliament passed this legislation it had not its eyes open.
A portion of the Act which has been read by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals shows that we retained all these powers.

I contended before and I contend again that we are discussing a difficulty that does not exist in this matter Mr. DAVIS.
at all. A question I would like to have answered is with regard to this 720 miles of railway that we are dealing with in this Bill. What control does the Manitoba government contend that it has, or what control has it, or can it possibly have in regard to this proposition we are dealing with ? Has the government of Manitoba any control over it ? These 720 miles of new road are not affected at all by the bargain made between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Manitoba government two yeans ago.
This is all outside of Manitoba.
Y'es, we have the matter clouded to some extent by the fact that there is a general provision for the control of rates by the commission.

I will inform the hon. gentleman what portion the province of Manitoba have control of under this Bill. They have control from Port Arthur to the crossing of the Rainy river, from Winnipeg to the southerly boundary of Manitoba, from Gladstone to Winnipegosis, from Sifton Junction upwards on that part that is iii Manitoba; they have control over the Emerson branch and from Beaver to Gladstone.
Is this government guaranteeing any of these S
These are the roads which are included in this Bill, and the Manitoba government have control over them under their contract.
We are dealing with 720 miles of railway which are not yet built.
Y'ou have not read the Act, Sir.

You have read a schedule of the property that is going to be mortgaged by the Canadian Northern Railway for the money advanced.
Mr, SCOTT. Will my hon. friend from Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) indicate what control the Manitoba government have over these 720 miles ?
That is in the agreement which was confirmed by this government.
There was never anything confirmed about that 720 miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The leader of the opposition has answered all that, and I' do not wish to take up time discussing it.

We are discussing a difficulty which does not enter into this at all. Suppose we strike out clause 6 entirely, then the position or the law with respect to public control of rates is not changed in the least.

Does not the provision that the control of all lines owned by the Canadian Northern Railway shall be in the Governor in Council; does not that cover portions of the Canadian Northern Railway which are in the contract between the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the province of Manitoba ?
Would you like to have that struck out ?
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I say is that if you wipe that out altogether it does not make any difference. We have this matter mixed up with the Smendment which the Minister of Railways suggested regarding certain maximum rates. I may say, without any breach of faith, that it was upon the representation made by supporters of the government from west of Lake Superior that the provision for maximum rates lias been suggested by the Minister of Railways and Canals. These maximum rates, so far as I can understand, are not intended to refer to any traffic originating upon the line under the partial control of the government of Manitoba, but entirely with regard to traffic originating upon this 720 miles of railway that has not yet been built, and that the government of Manitoba has nothing to do with.
Suppose we agree to strike out all the portions of that clause that are so offensive to lion, gentlemen opposite, will they let the Bill pass and let us get on with some useful business ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Oil, you can put it through without any amendment or anything else.
The MINISTER OF; RAILWAYS AND CANALS. My hon. friend says that, because he knows that his whole contention is without foundation and is an absolute waste of time.
What is your suggestion ?

Let it read :
The rates and tolls to be charged for the transfer of freight and passengers upon the lines of railway so aided shall not in any case be higher than the rates and tolls which may be fixed in the contract to be made between the government of Canada and the Canadian Northern Railway under this Act.
If this clause be amended in that way, and if you strike out all reference to the other lines owned' by the Canadian Northern Railway and strike out the statement that they shall be under the control of the government of Canada it is all the same tiling. If my hon. friends opposite think it will alter the matter, and that it will suit them, and they will let the section through, I am perfectly willing to strike these words out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The minister still does not provide that it shall be in the direction of preserving the contract between the Manitoba government and the Canadian Northern Railway.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS, AND CANALS. What business have you to put that in ?
.Mr. LANCASTER. I cannot see for the life of me why the amendment of the leader of the opposition should not be accepted. If the minister is going to do anything that will have the result of repealing any agreement which this House has sanctioned, it is a most extraordinary thing. Could the province of Manitoba in equity repeal that bargain that they have made with the Canadian Northern Railway ?
They made the bargain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That bargain would have no legal effect unless it were endorsed by the authority of this parliament, and in equity we are in the same position as the province of Manitoba.
Not at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then we should not have passed, the Act ?
Not at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would, the hon. member allow me to give him an instance ? My attorney in Edmonton sends me a legal document to transfer land, for my signature and I sign it. I was a party to the bargain, but it had no effect until I got a notary public to certify to the signature.

That has nothing to do with it, but I will give a parallel case. Suppose my hon. friend is an executor of an estate and his consent is required to the sale of land belonging to the heirs and the heirs selling does he mean to say that after he gives consent he can turn around next year and say that he had power to repudiate it ?
It is not the same tiling at all.

It is exactly the same. Here is a contract between the province of Manitoba and a railway and it is no earthly use to that railway unless the Dominion parliament sanctioned it. The parties come to the Dominion parliament and get it sanctioned, and can the Dominion parliament turn around a year or'two afterwards and try to reserve their right to break it ? If there is any equity in the matter at all this parliament should stick to the bargain which it endorsed. As the leader of the opposition has said we may have the power in strict law to break that bargain, or we may have power as a parliament if

we wish to use it, to do a most inequitable thing, but there is no court of equity or uo court of conscience which would rule that we could break a bargain which we solemnly entered into.
Did the hon. member give his support to that endorsation by this House ?
What difference does that make ?
It does not make any difference as a matter of fact.
This parliament did it as a whole.

At the very time we gave that endorsation to that bargain and as part of that endorsation we said :	We do
not change our attitude or our control. That statement was as much a part of the endorsation as the other part of it.

In equity that could not amount to anything more than our waving our specific right to deal with that particular matter about which we were legislating, but still retaining our rights generally. We must have meant something when we passed that endorsation, and what we did was to preserve our rights generally in regard to similar matters, while we waived our right in that particular instance.

If the exception was intended surely the exception would have been stated, but as a matter of fact, no exception was made and the wording covered everything as far as the English language could be made to do so.

Does the hon. gentleman mean that we were not confirming anything that had been done by Manitoba ? Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the exception was so wide that although we passed an Act concerning a certain agreement we did not mean anything ?
It means just what it said. I claim that the endorsation of that agreement meant exactly what we said.
What was that please ?
That we gave effect to that agreement without prejudice to our right to control, whenever we chose to exercise it.
That you gave effect to the agreement without prejudice to breaking it the next day.
Precisely; that was precisely the meaning of the words; that was the argument made in the Railway Committee; that was the understanding that was arrived at; there is no doubt about it.

The hon. minister promised to give us an account of the char-Mr. LANCASTER.
aeter of the road which is to be built, the gradients running west and east, and a general description.

The grading will be 26 feet to the mile going east and will not exceed 52 feet going west. The curvature is very favourable but I cannot give the maximum.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
