House again in Committee of Supply.
Department of Public Works-contingencies, further amount required, $7,500.
['I apologize.\nBill reported.']

When the vote of $10,000 in the main estimates was taken, it was found that there was an expenditure of over $8,000 yet unpaid, and it wras necessary to provide this vote in order to make up the amount required for the current year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: I suppose this is not paid yet ?
The principle amount due is to the stationery department for printing, &c.
That seems an enormous sum out of the whole vote of $18,000 and nearly all in the Stationery Department.

Year after year the vote has not been large enough to meet the liabilities. At the end of the year 1901-2, there was a balance of $8,376 of an overdraft.. That was at once deducted from the amount of the vote of $10,000, leaving only a small sum for the year's service. [DOT]
I suppose the hon. gentleman has the contingencies remaining unpaid, what are the principal ones ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I find that this item wras voted the other night and consequently there is nothing before the House.

Has the hon. miuis-ter made provision for the full payment of these contingencies in the estimates for next year, or will he again come down with supplementary estimates ? It would be better to ask for an amount sufficient to cover the appropriation required for 1903-4, so that the House will understand how much really is required by the government.

My instructions to the officers were to make up accounts in full, and next year I shall take particular care to see that the necessary amount required for this service is procured.

River Kaministiquia, dredging, $24,706.15.
Is this under contract 7
This money has been all spent and is due for dredging on the Kaministiquia river. The amount still due is $24,706.15.

Is this not an extraordinary proceeding-first to spend the money and then ask for an appropriation 7 I gave warning a year or two ago, when an item similar to this came up, that in future I would move that the item be struck out. I do not think that we are here simply to register the acts of the government in the expenditure of public money. We are here to consent to that expenditure, in the first place, aijd I hope that the hon. minister , will takfe ample provision for all he requires in the future and not ask parliament to be simply a registering body. I take no exception to the expenditure, because the Kaministiquia river is one of the most important harbours in the country. With the possible exception of Quebec and Vancouver there is no harbour more important.
An lion. MEMBER. And Halifax.
No, Halifax isn't in it. A great deal of money will probably have to be expended on the Kaministiquia in the future, because the country will demand it.

I have no objection to take to the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Henderson). This is undoubtedly one of the great works of the country. As the department has not sufficient money appropriated, perhaps, it was justified in spending more than was voted. However, I do not say there is any reason why we should be again in that position. It is far better to ask for the amount required. As to this particular work, I have asked the officers of the department to make full provision in the estimates, so that parliament may be seized of the exact amount we intend to spend.
The appropriation for 1902-3 for dredging was $35,000. Has this amount of $24,700 been spent in addition 7

That was another case of paying out of appropriation what was spent the year before. The full amount was not intended for the current year. My desire was to find out exactly how the accounts stand and make provision in the supplementary estimates, and to take a vote for next year for all that will be necessary.
I did not understand the hon. minister to answer the question asked by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett). Was this work done by contract or by the yard 7 Who were the contractors 7

This work has all been done at fifteen cents per yard. 1 think the amount is principally due to the Great Lakes Dredging Company. I have here a full plan of the works which I will lay on the Table.
Trails, roads and bridges-Yukon Territory- To pay account of Trading and Exploring Company, Limited, for transportation of men from Hutchiku on the Yukon river to Lake Labarge, in September, 1899, $481.

This is to pay the travelling expenses of thirteen men, as stated in the item, being at the rate of $37 per man. The amo. nt has not been paid sooner, owing to the delay in procuring a properly certified account to be passed by the Auditor General. These parties live in Dawson, and it was a matter of communication between the department, the Auditor General's Department, and the parties having the claim. The account duly certified having been received, the vote had lapsed. This vote is to pay the amount.
Telegraph lines-Quesnel-Atlin section of main line and Port Simpson-Hazelton and 150 Mile House-Quesnel Forks (Horse-fly) branches -additional amount for construction, $20,000.

This is to settle outstanding accounts in connection with this telegraph line. The deputy minister informs me that lie believes this will pay the construction accounts in full. If the committee desire, I can give the details of the amounts to be paid.
Is this another case of the previous year's estimate being exceeded, or is it a case of paying one year's expenditure out of the following year's appropriation 7

Both statements might be partly correct, but I do not understand either to be wholly so. An appropriation was not taken for the amount necessary, but this particular vote is to pay accounts which did not come in in time to be paid out of the vote.
Is this under contract 7
These are unpaid accounts under contract.
Did any portion of these items relate to the year 1901-2 7
I think they were all contracted for in that year.
I suppose the hon. minister will have no objection to their going before the Public Accounts Committee 7
No, if there is to be an investigation, I think all these accounts ought to go.
Are extensive repairs going on upon this line ?
No, only the usual repairs.
What is the condition of the line ?
The information received by the department is that the line is in fairly good condition.
I notice an item in the western papers that a party of men has been sent out to reconstruct the line at different points.
That is not correct.
By whom are the repairs being carried out 1
There is a staff of line men located along the line.

The damage to the line is reported as being very serious, and, as the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has said, it is reported that a party of men have gone out to make extensive repairs. It was suggested by the late Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that one portion of the line it was almost impossible to keep in repair, and it was proposed to overcome the difficulty by laying a cable. It was reported in the western papers that a party had gone out under the direction of the gentleman who constructed the line, to make repairs. Is there anything in that ?
As I have said, there is no knowledge of it in the department. There is no foundation for the statement.
Will the hon. minister give us the receipts of the line ?

There will be an item later, on which that will more properly come up, and I have promised to give a full statement of the details.
Public works-chargeable to income-public buildings, Nova Scotia-Arichat public building, $4,800.
Has this building been completed V	*
Yes. This is to pay the balance of the contract.
What has been the cost of the building ?
Including heating and fittings, $8,813.65.
I have no recollection of this vote having been up before, but it seems the money was voted in a preceding year. Though it may be a little late to

protest, it is well to let the public know what is being done here. At this place, Arichat, in the county of Richmond, the population I think is under 600. The total receipts of the post office are $772, and the business is so insignificant that the Post Office Department would not allow the postmaster a single cent for the premises. Now the Department of Public Works are erecting a building at a cost of some $11,000 or $12,000. Would the minister tell us what purposes are to be served by this office, and [DOT]what remuneration will be paid to the caretaker ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC! WORKS. The building has been completed. The revenue of the post office is $772.75, and the customs revenue is $1,520.74. I suppose this is the chief town in that county, and the trade seems to be considerable. While the revenue from the post office seems small compared with that of larger centres, the amount of money orders issued was over $45,000.
Will there be a caretaker appointed for this building ?
An arrangement has been made with the postmaster to take charge of this building. A very small allowance, if any, will be given to him.

The minister says that the revenue from customs was sufficient to justify this expenditure. Does he consider that an income of $1,500 a year is a considerable income for a customs house ? As a matter of fact, that would represent the duty on about $6,000 worth of goods, an amount which an ordinary business man would bring in in one importation. And yet the hon. gentleman is putting up a building costing $11,000 or $12,000-$8,000 up to date, and $4,000 to be added.
No, the building is completed at a total cost of $8,813.
Well, even $8,000 is an outrageous cost. Besides, there is the salary of the caretaker. The expenditure is out of all proportion to the amount of revenue received at that place.
I understand that the previous government had a building there which became useless.
Because you own a small piece of land in the town of Arichat, worth perhaps a couple of hundred dollars, is it necessary to utilize it by putting up a building at a cost of $8,000 or $9,000 ?
There had been a building there before owned by the Dominion government.

I can give the committee a little information. In 1882, the

Conservative government bought a piece of land, and an old hardware shop about seventy years old for a post office. After that had been used for some time as a post office, we thought it was time to build a new one. We did not build it very large, and we built it to suit the requirements of the place. There should be no objection to it unless you want to use the old building for another seventy years.
What is the population of the place ?
You can find that out by the census.
The population of Aricliat and of West Arlchat are about 2,000.
Is the post office in Arichat or in West Aricbat ?
There is' a mail going to West Arichat from the Arichat post office.
How far apart are the two places ?
About four miles.

So this post office at Arichat cannot accommodate the people of West Arichat. The government built a post office at a little place with a population of 590 souls simply because at one time they owned a lot of land there and a wooden building.
When was the first vote voted ?
In 1901-2, $4,000 was voted.

I think this is a case where the opposition have a right to object. The government come forward and ask for an appropriation of $4,000 for the purpose of constructing a public building in that town, and before the building is completed we are asked to vote more than double that amount. I ami of the opinion that when a building is to be constructed the department should tell us what it is likely to cost before they ask us to undertake its construction.

It was not stated in the beginning what the total cost of the building would be, because it was not known. But so long as parliament is made aware of the amount o'f the obligation that is quite sufficient to justify parliament in voting the money. _ There are many works undertaken by this department as well as others for which the full amount is not asked at first, but so long as parliament is told what the estimatea cost of the work would be, that is usually considered a sufficient reason for undertakingthe work. In this case the amount of the contract was $4,400.

I suppose it is fair to assume that that is the amount the govern-183 i
ment intended to expend upon the building. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would tell us how it is that the extras are more than the first contract.
The estimates of three years ago were less than the estimates of the same work would be now. Lumber has almost doubled in price.
The most of this work was done two years ago, $3,000 of this was spent in 1901-2. It is not the present prices we are dealing with.
The money was voted then, but it was not spent.

I think that my statement that the contract was $4,400 is somewhat misleading. The amount of the contract for the building was $4,400, but then there was heating, which cost $1,038, fittings and letter boxes, which cost $2,074; fencing and sidewalks, $200, and incidentals $157.20.
What proportion was done by contract out of the full amount ?
The whole of it was done by contract.
What kind of heating is there in this building ?
Hot water.

The difficulty is that when coming before parliament and asking for a vote the statement is made by the minister that a building is to cost only so much money, and then when complaint was made that it is costing more, the answer is : We have spent so much money and we must finish it. We had a glaring example of this in the Grande Vallee expenditure. In that case the first amount asked for was $5,000. It was supposed by the committee that that .was all that would be required, but the expenditure since has amounted to over $60,000. If the officers of the department are competent, as I believe they are, because I do not think the fault lies with them, when an expenditure is asked for we should have before this committee an exact estimate of the final cost of the building or work upon which the money is to be expended. As far as the enhanced price of building material is concerned, it is certainly not sufficient to account for the difference between the sum asked for and the sum expended in this case. It is true that building materials have advanced in price, but not more than 25 per cent, although the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Mathesom told us that in his part of the country they had advanced 100 per cent in price.

I have no reason to know that this estimate was not given when this vote was asked for. The practice in the department is that

the chief architect always furnishes the minister, when the estimates are sent down, with an estimate in detail as to what in his opinion the work will cost. There is no reason why that should not he submitted to parliament, and I quite agree with the principle contended for by the hon. gentleman.

I would like to ask the hon. minister why the government finds it necessary to expend $8,000 for a public building in a village with population not quite 600 ? Is the government prepared to adopt that as a policy ? If it is, we have in the province of Ontario hundreds of villages with a greater population than that mentioned here in which there are no public buildings. Is it because the hon. member, representing this particular constituency, has a special pull that the public fund should be spent in this way? Is it the intention of the government to pursue this course in the future ?
Perhaps this government, to a certain extent, is treading in the path of its predecessor. The hon. gentleman must know that when his party were in power there were cases of this kind.
There were no cases as bad as this.

Is that the best justification the hon. minister is able to offer for an expenditure of $8,500 for a public building in a place of this kind ? The fittings that have gone into this building must be most palatial, because we find that $2,000 have been spent for letter boxes and fittings. I believe if you go through the province of Ontario you will find no such buildings as this even in towns with 4,000 inhabitants ; yet no expenditure in the province of Nova Scotia is considered too large to keep this constituency politically safe.

WTiat are these fittings ? With a population of 600 in the village it is costing $4 per head to put up this public building. What do these fittings consist of ? Have you furnished rooms in this building for the population ? And is there a ball room there ?
The fittings are the usual fittings to be found in public buildings throughout the Dominion.
Would it not strike the hon. minister that these fittings are a little above the usual class of fittings when it cost $2,000 to fit up a post office, the building of which cost $4,400 ?

The fittings and the furniture would be very much the same as they would be in a much more expensive building, unless the building was a very much larger one. I Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
think this is a very fair proportion having regard to the expenditure of the building.
How many boxes are there ?
There is a bonded warehouse in the basement, and there is a place for the collector of customs.
Have you anything in that bonded warehouse ?
Yes, the necessary fittings.
What necessary fittings would be in a bonded warehouse ?
Then, there is the savings bank department, and the janitor's room.

This is a very extraordinary expenditure. Figured out it means that for every head of the population in that town of $600-and it is a little village if the hon. gentleman will pardon me for calling it a village, because in Ontario it would be considered a very small village-this country is bribing that village, and incidentally the whole riding with an expenditure of $15. The hon. Minister of Public Works can figure it out, and if he is going to proportion the bribe to the whole Dominion with public buildings, it will only cost $00,000,000. I am going to ask the hon. minister to consider an application from the town of Midland for a public building. Its population is 4,500, and on behalf of the hon. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), and in pursuance of an old promise, I am going to ask for cold justice for the town of Owen Sound. The hon. gentleman will perhaps recollect the promise made in his behalf that if he was elected in the riding of North Grey they would get a post office building. They have not got it yet.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett), says that this expenditure was made to bribe a constituency to secure it for the government, and then he says that we should bribe Midland in his riding, I suppose, so that the government might carry it, and that we should bribe Owen Sound, so that my hon. friend who represents it now (Mr. Thomson. North Grey) may not come back. Is that the hon. gentleman's logic ?

I am quite willing that the hon. gentleman should go into the constituency of East Simcoe and expend all the money they wish, because some of the expenditures they have made in that constituency I have protested against on the floor of this House. You wasted three or four thousand dollars of public money on a dock in the village of Hawkestone, and you so disgusted the decent Liberals there that I had a less majority against me than ever before.

The government the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) supiiorted bought an old hardware shop In Arichat when they were in power, and they promised to give us a post office but they never did so. I do not see why the gentlemen from Ontario should be so jealous of a little money being spent in Arichat. Arichat was a flourishing town before Midland had a man in it civilized enough to wear clothes.

I am afraid that the minister is being so hard pressed that I shall be obliged to come to his rescue. In bygone years I advocated the construction of post offices in towns of from 1,500 to 2,000 population throughout the country. I consider that the government would save money in the rentals which they have to pay, and they could procure abundance of money to build these post offices at three per cent. In place of an old frame building that has been used for some other purpose for seventy years, you could have a substantial brick or stone building with a fireproof vault. But there is no reason in the world why the government should not erect a post office in that town of Arichat for $5,000 or $6,000, sufficient for the requirements of the place and containing a residence for the postmaster so that there would be no expense for the caretaker. The policy is all right, but the working out of this policy by the government is all wrong. That policy should have a general application. I do not know of any more popular or more profitable undertaking that the government could engage in, than the erection of public buildings of that kind all over the country. I hope, however, that the minister will not confine his attention to the old antiquated town of Arichat. If it be true that it was in existence long before the white man settled in Midland, it must be an unprogressive and decayed old town, if it has not a population of more than 600 now. I trust it is not a sample of the whole county of Richmond, because if the county be as unprogressive as the town, there is no doubt that the government thought it necessary to do something to keep the place alive by constructing this building. But what I do say is that it is monstrous to spend $2,000 for fittings in a post office to supply 600 people. There are hundreds of towns in the province of Ontario more populous than Arichat which have very inconvenient buildings for post offices. In the morning and evening when the mails arrive in these towns, the congestion is so great that it is almost impossible far a person to get his letters, and yet no public building is erected 'n these Ontario towns, while an old antiquated place like Arichat, which seems to be dying of decay, and where there is not enough people to make a crowd when the mails arrive, gets a post office building which costs over $8,000. I favour the policy of erecting public buildings in progressive towns and I hope the minister will carry out that policy, but as I .have said, it is monstrous to spend $8,000 for a post office building in a town of a population of 600. I believe the Minister of Public Works himself commended some years ago the very policy that I am advocating now. I know the member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser) did, but he is not here to-night.
Oh, yes I am.

I am very glad he is here, because I see that we will be called upon in a few minutes to vote for a public building in Guysborough, and the hon. gentleman is manly enough to be here to defend what may possibly be a job something like that which is to be perpetrated in Arichat. I think, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Holmes) that you yourself advocated the very policy that 1 am advocating now, but some mistake was made in the carrying out of that policy in Clinton. It was all right to erect a post office in Clinton which would cost $6,000 as was first proposed, but if my memory serves me right they spent somewhere about $15,000 on that post office in the end. I will not undertake to say whether it was the member (Mr. Holmes) or the minister that was at fault, but anyway they spoiled the Vhole plan and instead of spending $6,000 as might have been spent in the public interest, they worked out the policy so that they spent $15,000, which was to that extent, an absolute waste of public money. I hope the minister will take warning from what has been said, and that he will cut off something of the fittings-
And spoil the job.

The member for West York (Mr. Campbell), has spoiled many things. He is trying to spoil the market gardeners at Toronto. He would not vote to help them in anyway, but he is perfectly willing to endorse an expenditure of $8,000 for a post office in a little town of 600 population away down in Nova Scotia. What strange things the member for West York (Mr. Campbell) will do at times. I trust that the Minister of Public Works will erect public buildings at a moderate cost in many thriving towns in the Dominion, but I do hope that he will not spend such large sums of money as this vote indicates in carrying out that policy.
'I was very much pleased with the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Henderson).
Hear, hear.

The Conservative government promised a post office in Arichat and they did not build it, and they ran the Conservative majority down to only twenty-one, that was against me. and I presume that their speeches to-night will kill that twenty-one as dead as Julius Caesar.
Are they all for sale there ?

If they were all for sale you would have more of them than you have. The Conservative government bought the property and they promised a post office, but they never fulfilled their promise, and they yvould leave the post mistress to stand on the ice all winter.
Who promised the post office ?
The Conservative party bought an old hardware shop for n site in 1882.
Oh !

I am rather surprised to hear the hon. members for East Simcoe and Halton, who have been so many years voting estimates, such as $15,000 for the Marysville post office, objecting to this item. At Marysville they built a post office which cost some $15,000 and where the revenue is only $350 a year.
What is the population of Marysville ?
Four or five hundred.
It is 1,400.

The* late government spent $15,000 on the post office there, and there were many other instances of a similar nature in the days gone by which never drew a word of protest from these hon. gentlemen, but now because there is an item for a post office in the town of Arichat, which is the centre for that whole county, they are very indignant.

On referring to the census returns for York, it will be seen that the hon. gentleman is about as near to the facts as he usually is. He makes the statement that in Marysville the population is 500, where the population is 1,400.
When the post office was built some ten, years ago, the population was only 500.

I do not think there is a public building in the county of Grey built by the government. Let me give a list of the towns and their population in this county. Meaford with a population of 1,960, has no public building. Shelburue, with a population of 1,188, has no public building. Thornbury, with a population of 900, has no public building. Owen Sound, with a population of 9.000, has no public building. Hanover, with a population of 1,300, has no public building. Durham, with a population of 1,392, has no public building.
Which of those are county towns ?

Owen Sound is the county town of Grey. Markdale with Mr. MATHESON.
a population of 892, has no public building. Yet we find here in a small place of 590 population, the government has spent $8,500. There must be something radically wrong, when such an insignificant place is to have so expensive a building and when all these much larger places I have fiien-tioned have not received such consideration. If the government are prepared to adopt the principle that each place like Arichat should have a public building, we are satisfied, but lam not prepared to vote such heavy expenditures in places like this when towns five or six times as large are not to have any public buildings. The government has oceans of money to spend on these little insignificant places but nothing in the larger centres.

It has been represented that Arichat is a very small insignificant place and further that when this vote was originally proposed, the amount then estimated was but $4,000. If hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to look back, they will find that when this vote was originally proposed the estimate was very much in excess of $4,000. I have a distinct recollection of that vote when first submitted. Arichat is not so broken down a place as the hon. member for Halton would have us believe. Look at the money transactions. You will find that $45,819.10 were sent from that post office in money orders alone during the past year. That is a respectable volume of business. 1 think the government is perfectly justified in making ample provision for the conduct of business of that kind.
Then there is the customs house besides.

I am simply speaking of the business done in the post office, and if hon. gentlemen will study the returns they will find that Arichat is after all not so insignificant. If the hon. member for Halton would turn to the great province of Ontario, he will find very few towns that do more business in money orders Will he find half a dozen or a dozen ?
Hundreds.
I stand quite willing to be corrected.
That money order business may be accounted for by this circumstance. You probably have not got a bank there ?
Yes, there is a bank there, the Union Bank of Halifax, one of the best institutions in the country.

I desire to say ill reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton that the statements I made -with reference to Arichat, which he thinks not quite fair, were based on the remarks made by himself. He told us the age of this building,

how long the town had existed, and I concluded that it must be a very uuprogressive place or it would have to-day a population of more than GOO.
But I took good care to state that the Conservative party had neglected it.

The hon. gentleman said the late government made a promise, which shows that they were not neglecting it. It would appear, however, from wuat the hon. gentleman said, that after sending an engineer down there to investigate, the late government considered the place was not of such importance as demanded the expenditure required by the erection of a post office.
Are you quoting facts or drawing from your imagination ?

I think the hon. gentleman has been drawing very largely on his imagination. What I said was a fair deduction from the remarks of the hon. i gentleman from Richmond, and I do not j think I should be held responsible, if there I is anything wrong in what I did say. Two or three nights ago I had occasion to bring up a matter very much similar, where a promise had been made of a public work in my own county at the time of an election. That same thing seems to have been doue in Nova Scotia. 1 asked the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to implement that promise. I do not care whether it was made properly or improperly, once a promise of that kind is made to the electors, the government should keep faith with them. I have not objected to the erection of a post office in Arichat. I approve of the policy of erecting post offices in small towns, but not in towns where there are only 500 or 600 people. Where there are 1,000 or 2,000,
I believe in the policy of erecting public buildings, because the interest on the cost would simply take the place of the rental. The policy is good, but it is worked out badly in the case of Arichat. The government might have a very suitable post office, which would meet all requirements, for $2,000 or $3,000 less money.

The more you look into this matter the more serious it appears. The total revenue from this post office at Arichat is $772, and the salaries and commissions amount to $533, giving a net revenue of $232. If you compute $8,000 at 4 per cent, you get $320, which, you are going to pay a year on a post office which only nets you a revenue of $230. The postal revenue at Owen Sound is $14,400, and the total expenses are $4,500, leaving a net revenue of $10,000, and yet Owen Sound has no public building. In Meaford the postal revenue is $3,199, and the expenditure $1,255; leaving a net revenue of $2,000. I merely mention these facts to show that we are putting up a building in this partiW
cular place where, judging by its postal revenue and business, there is none required and no demand for it except for political purposes.

It has been alleged by hon. gentlemen opposite that a good deal more money is spent on these buildings in Nova Scotia than in Ontario. I give that statement a most emphatic denial. It has been the policy of governments in tLe past to put up these public buildings in county towns.
Is Arichat a county town S

Yes, it is the county town. The building is completed, and will accommodate the post office savings bank, the post office, the collector of customs, bonded warehouse, tide-waiters, Ac. It costs a good deal to complete a building of decent proportions for these services. I would like hon. gentlemen opposite to understand that there are as many towns 1 i proportim throughout Nova Scotia which have not post office accommodation as there are in the province of Ontario. For instance, there is the town of Arichat West, and, in my own county, the town of Bridgetown
Is it a county town V

Arichat is the county town. There are only two towns in Nova Scotia, so far as I know, that are not county towns that have buildings, and in those cases the buildings were put up by the late government. In the town of Annapolis, which had a population of little over 900, the late government put up a large and expensive building, but they did not build one in Bridgetown, which, I think, was quite as large or larger. The reason assigned at the time was that Annapolis was the shire town and so entitled to the building. The town of Lunenburg, with a population of about 2,000, has a building erected which cost $45,000, but the neighbouring town of Bridgewater, with a population of over 1,800 has no post office building even to the present time. The policy was adopted^ by the late government of building post offices in the shire towns first, the other towns being supposed to come in for consideration afterwards. It does seem to me that if the late government purchased the site for this building and promised the people that the building would be constructed, hon. gentlemen opposite who say that the government should carry out its promises can hardly complain because the building is completed, particularly as the building is for the shire town of this county of Richmond.

I think it unfair that this should be spoken of as a post office simjily, when it is intended for a bonded warehouse, custom house, post office, savings bank, and telephone and telegraph

5S40
office. Allow for the rent of these different government offices and also for the rent that will he received from the telegraph and telephone companies, and I think it will he found that this building is a paying investment. This was started by the party of lion, gentlemen opposite who are now talking against it. But we were told all along : What is the use of expecting a building if you do not send a supporter of the government-that is of the late government. We sent a supporter, but we did not get the building. An lion, gentleman tells us that they sent an engineer to examine, and he reported that the building was not necessary. I would like to know where that report is. I asked the lion., gentleman who made the statement if he was drawing on his imagination or talking from facts. I suppose that if he were talking from facts, lie would be able to produce them; and as he does not do so, I would infer that he is drawing on his imagination. He says that all the information lie got about the town was from me. I am not aware that I said anything injurious to the town-
The hon. gentleman said the post mistress had cold feet.

And some bon. gentlemen opposite will have cold feet before they get into power again if they go on this way. It is not by repudiating their obligations that statesmen get along. This building is completed, and I do not think it would be businesslike now to repudiate it and refuse to pay the price. Yet, if lion, gentlemen ojiposite mean anything, that is what they mean. The town of Arichat was never considered a very insignificant town, though it must be confessed that part of the population left it during the eighteen sorrowful years when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. They are now citizens of the United .States, where they are well appreciated. But some of them are coming back now, and, with! improvements such as this building in the town, we hope to draw more of them.
Guysborough public building, $11,000.
The MINISTER 01" PUBLIC WORKS. This is to complete the payments for the building, the construction of which is finished.
What is the total cost ?

The population of Guysborough seems to be 1.400, and the government formerly rented premises for the post office for $40 a year. If the hon. minister intends to apply this method all over the country, the results will be far from pleasing.

Much that has been said about the county has been true of Guysborough. A building there serves in an im-Mr. MATHESON.
portant measure for the whole county. The population of the county is 18,000, and the county town is the centre where the court sits, the place of the savings bank, custom house, and so on. This is the beautiful building, and the postmaster appointed by the late government lives in the building, so that there will be no cost for caretaking. There is a railway now being built of about 200 miles.

Carried.
Mr. BLA1N. When was the first vote taken for this building, and when was the contract let and what was the price V
The first vote taken was in 1C01-2 and ti e total contract was $20,747.

I am surprised to hear the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) trying to offer a defence for an expenditure of this kind. Though I have only for a short time had the honour of a seat in this House, I have read the speeches of the hon. member with great pleasure, and always regarded him as an outspoken enemy of expenditures of this kind. I find that, accor iug to the public accounts, the total revenue of the post office in this town for last year was $990, while the expenditure for salaries and commissions wras $725. That is, the salaries and commissions amounted to very nearly as much as was received altogether. Yet this government is expending $20,000 for a post office building. And the hon. member for Guysborough defends it. And were it an expenditure in another constituency, it would not look so badly, but to defend such an expenditure for his own constituency it looks all the worse.
I never spoke against public buildings-
Oh, oh.

Never, I always thought it was a good idea. Now" I know that it is a good thing to have a building in each of the shire towns of Nova Scotia. It may not pay immediately, but eventually it will pay. This is a fine stone and brick building, standing on a very fine lot overlooking the harbour and so close that the ships can come right up to where the building is. I do not defend this because it is in my own county, for I never spoke against expenditures of this kind. I do object to buildings of this kind that were intended to bribe constituencies. Think of Lunenburg getting a building at a cost of $45,000. I did not say a word against it, for I thought that good judgment prevailed in that case. And I know that good judgment prevails here.

The hon. member says this is a county towm. Is he prepared to use his influence to get a building put up in Owen Sound, which is a

county town, with a population of 9,000 and a postal revenue of $15,000 V Will the hon. gentleman raise his voice in favour of justice being done to Owen Sound ?

Decidedly, I will not object-badly as Owen Sound is represented.
Middleton armoury (revote of $2,900 lapsed) $8,400.
This is required to complete the construction of the armoury at Middleton.
In what county is Middleton ? What is the population of the town and what the population of the county ?
It is in the county of Annapolis, and the population is 900.
What is the total cost of that building to be ?

Eight thousand five hundred.
Marysville, public building, $2,700.

This, I think, is the place that the hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Gibson) spoke of. I understood him to say that the money had been expended some years ago to put up a building here, but I see now there is a vote asked for a site for a building.
There was a revote taken several years ago, but it was not expended. The building is now completed, at a total cost of $13,233.
How long lias this been under construction 1
Since 1902.

I understood the hon. gentleman from York to say that some $15,000 had been expended by the late government. It is evident that lie could not have known what he was talking about.
Montmagny public buildings-Governor General's warrant, $2,800.

During the heavy storm at that place this building caved in and it was necessary to make repairs at once. My opinion is that it will be necessary to revote this and put up a new building. I am having it now investigated and reported upon.
Was the $2,,800 expended ?

No, it was not. I came to the conclusion when this accident happened and the roof fell in, and after having an investigation made by an architect, that it was not desirable to use the Governor General's warrant. We had some temporary repairs made,
and we will have to take a vote to pay the Governor General's warrant.
Was this building erected by the department, or was it purchased ?

I think it was purchased and largely improved by the department. I will have a full report made of it by the engineer.
Deseronto, public building, $4,500.

This is a very expensive building. The total cost is $40,555.50. This sum will complete that building.
Toronto post office-building for branch office in west end of city (station C), $10,500.
This completes the work. It was let by contract.
I would ask the minister to allow that to stand, if he has no objection. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), I think, wants to make some inquiries.

1 have no objection whatever.
Item allowed to stand.
Kingston Royal Military College-revote of $2,000 lapsed, $32,000.
This is to make provision for completion, during the fiscal year, of the gymnasium and residence. The amount of the contract was $35,956.
Will that complete everything ?

All the work under contract. I think there has been an application for some fittings, they will come down in the estimates far 1903-4.
Ottawa-for_the completion of the bacteriological laboratory for the cattle quarantine branch of the Department of Agriculture, $6,000.

That is the balance of the contract to complete the work.
Toronto, assistant receiver general's office, additional vault accommodation-Governor General's warrant, $1,500.

Representations were made by the Finance Department that the funds were in danger from the bad state of the building, and the need of repairs was so urgent that a Governor General's warrant was asked for. This is to make that good.
Ottawa, public buildings-electric lighting- for purchase of transformers installed in buildings on Parliament Hill and the Langevin block, inclusive of wiring in duets, &c., $11,000.
These transformers were supplied by the Ottawa Electric Company, at the time the electric light was put in.

We have several times been left in total darkness by the failure of the electric light. I must ask the minister what steps can be taken to prevent it in the future. Last night when we were here about 10 o'clock, the lights again went out. Has any investigation been made to determine the cause of the trouble last night, or on previous occasions ? There must be something defective. Whether the contract has not been properly carried out or whether there is something that cannot be overcome, I do not know, but I have no doubt the minister will give it his attention, so that we may not again be left in the uncomfortable position in which we have found ourselves on several occasions.

It is certainly very annoying to have the lights go out. An investigation has been made by the officials of the department, and we have ascertained that the difficulty has not arisen from any defect in this building, but the trouble has been at the power house of the electric company. 1 was informed myself by one of the officials of the company that it was owing to a defect in one of their switchboards, which has been remedied, and we may not fear any recurrence of the trouble in future. One thing we might adopt to prevent a recurrence of that trouble, would be to have a storage battery, but that would be very expensive. The chief architect has informed me that it might cost about ?70,000 to instal a storage battery, and as the company claim that they have discovered the cause of the accidents that have been happening during the present session, and that when a new switchboard has been put in the interruption to the service is not likely to happen again, I think we might give it another trial before undertaking such a large expenditure.

Has the hon. minister ever taken into consideration the question as to whether it would be more economical for the government to manufacture its own electricity instead of paying a company for supplying the current. To my mind, if the municipalities throughout the country find it profitable to put in electric plants to light up the towns and villages, we. with such a large extent of buildings here requiring so many lights, might well operate along the same lines. I have no doubt the hon. minister or some of his predecessors have had that under consideration. I dare say his officers can give us some information as to which would be likely to be the cheaper.
I have thought about the matter but I have

not had the investigation made that I intend to have made. Of course we have no water-power and a comparison would have to be made as to the cost of instituting a steam plant and as to whether a saving could be effected under those circumstances. It is a matter that will receive attention during the coming season. I think the cost will be rather high ? I will ask the chief architect and the officials of the department to look into the matter and see if any saving can be effected.
I think the difficulty last night was caused by the severe storm passing over the city.
Yes, and I am informed by one of the officials of the company that it was on account of the switchboard being out of order.

I am surprised to hear the hon. Minister of Public Works say that the government could not make a comparison because they have no water-power. Do I understand that all of the water-power has passed out of the hands of the government ? Surely such a magnificent property as the water-power has not been all disposed of by the government or passed beyond their control entirely ? If it is so I very much regret it because it is something that no doubt parliament could have utilized to very great advantage. Perhaps the hon. minister made a slip when he made that statement. I would be very glad to know whether that is really the case.

I am afraid it is too true that these water-powers were not thought to be of so much value and that they passed out of the hands of the crown many years ago. However, the matter will receive consideration. I do not suppose they thought of lighting this building with electricity when it was first built ?
Ottawa post office and customs house-fitting up examining warehouse and putting in electric elevator ; also alterations and improvements in post office. $6,500.
This is to complete the payment on the contracts for improvements made to the Ottawa post office.

Certainly they were not made before they were required.
Manitoba-Winnipeg immigration buildings- isolation hospital (revote of lapsed amount), $6,200.

Has the hon. minister ever taken into consideration the terrible risk that people are put to who may be housed in the immigration building near the Canadian Pacific Railway station at Winnipeg ? On viewing it last autumn it struck me that on almost any occasion a

fire might take place amongst the old wooden structures there, and so in a particular structure of this kind with the means of getting in and out some terrible calamity might occur at any time. I hope before too much money is spent in repairing a building of this kind the government will take into consideration, the propriety of having one erected on some other site where there will be less danger from fire.

Ltepresentations were made to the department and are now under consideration. I think the urgency of providing a better service there would perhaps require a new building altogether. It will be necessary,
I think, in the interests of the public that we should have a new building. It may be possible before the supplementary estimates come down that we will have plans to submit to the House showing what is proposed to be done.
Ottawa public buildings-gas and electric light. $2,500.
Where is the gas.

Right here.
Ail hon. MEMBER. It's ail outside of the chamber.
I am not joking. Why is not the gas turned on to the building so that we may have it when the electric lights go out.

All you have to do is to light a match.
Some resolutions reported.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 207) to prohibit the importation, manufacture or
sale of adulterated, process or renovated butter, oleomargarine, butterine or other substitutes for butter ; and to prevent the improper marking of butter/-The Minister of Agriculture.

I beg leave to move that section 4 be struck out and the following substituted :
No person shall import into Canada, offer, sell or have in his possession for sale any butter containing over 16 per cent of water.
My object is to give this clause the same form as the succeeding one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher).

speechtext: What was the form in which it passed the committee before ?
This does not change the meaning of the clause, but only the form.
The percentage is the same as in the English Act ?
Exactly.

When the Bill was up before the House the other day, I had not the information before me to enable me to speak intelligently on the subject. During the past few days, however, I received from Winnipeg protests against the measure from the firm of Messrs. Reid, Rice & Company, produce packers and exporters of butter. In the older provinces there are creameries at convenient points, but in Manitoba and the Territories we have but few creameries. The farms are larger, generally half a section, thus requiring half a mile distance to cross which makes it difficult to use the creameries. It is true that in the Territories, along the Calgary and Edmonton line and the Manitoba and North-western, the government had come to to the rescue of the farmers and established creameries, but in Manitoba there are but few creameries. In that province we have at present a very large number of Galicians. Mennonites, and" other foreigners, as well as natives of the country, who live largely on the products of the ten or fifteen cows which each one possesses, and who besides are able to make a certain quantity of butter for sale. This butter is not up to the standard required for export or the standard in the creamery. I can well recollect a few years ago a certain dealer in butter from Scotland, who went among the Mennonites to see the butter they made. He had photographed in Winnipeg an invoice of some of this butter, which he had bought at the rate of three cents a pound. This quality of butter, although made from pure milk, is not worth more than seven to ten cents a pound, and it is sold to the dealers at that rate. This firm established itself in Winnipeg for the purpose of buying this butter. The butter is not adulterated in any

way, but it is as pure as any butter in the market. Going through a certain process of boiling, purifying and cooling, the butter is so improved that they are able to sell it at fifteen or sixteen cents per pound. They tell me that this butter is so improved that it will keep as long, or longer, than the butter made in the creamery. They sell it in large quantities to railway camps and other large consumers. And, owing to this process, the manufacturers are able to pay the farmers a much higher price for this class of butter than could otherwise be paid. I think that all desirable purposes would be attained if this Bill were restricted to cover only the butter for export, while butter sold for home consumption should be allowed to go through the process I have spoken of and be sold without restriction. I do not know whether the minister has had under consideration this phase of the Bill, but I can tell him it will seriously affect the county I live in, as well as the county represented by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. LaRivi&re), especially the Mennonites there, who manufacture large quantities of butter. It is true they do not know how to manufacture it well, but they are trying to learn as quickly as they can. But if this Bill passes they will be at the mercy of store keepers and others, and will be compelled to sell their butter at three, four or five cents a pound, as they did some years ago. I would bring this to the attention of the hon. minister, and would ask hon. members here, who are conversant with the subject, to give their ideas upon the points involved.

I have gone into this matter, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) suggests, very thoroughly. I have stated already in the House very plainly the necessity for the provisions of the Bills which strike at the manufacture in Canada of process butter.
T do not think that the House has cavilled, much, if at all, at the stand I have taken on this subject. The hon. gentleman speaks of one particular firm in Manitoba that manufactures this process butter. I knew of that firm before I undertook to frame this Bill, and it was partly in consequence of representations which came from the creamery men in the province of Manitoba-

They are jealous, of course.
'The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. They are jealous of the reputation of their own butter. [DOT]

That is doubtful.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE -that I was led to go into the matter more carefully in regard to the province of Manitoba. The description which the hon. gentleman has given of this manufacture, I think, clearly illustrates the danger involved in this process to our general dairying trade. My hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) sug-Mr. McCREARY
gests that these provisions should only apply to the export trade. I do not think that is possible, for we can never tell where butter which is once allowed to be made and put upon the market will end. Butter may be made intended for the retail trade at home, but if the retail market happened to be a little quiet, the butter will immediately be sent forward for export. My hon. friend says that this process serves the purpose of helping the farmer. The dairy interest in this country is the one in which the farmers are more interested than in any other ; and the great export trade in dairying products in this country is the foundation of the prosperity of our dairy market. If we had not that splendid export trade, all our butter in this country would have to be sold at the low prices which my hon. friend mentioned, for, without the export trade, our production would flood the home market to such an extent that we could not possibly sell our butter at prices profitable to the maker. It is true, perhaps, that some few people in the country are making such a poor grade of butter that they cannot sell it at any price at all, but, by this process they would be able to foist upon the market at home an article which was not good to begin with and which, by the process under description may have been made to appear better, but is not made better permanently or really.
Does the hon. minister mean to say that you cannot improve butter or pork or any of these lines of goods- even milk-by process of boiling and purifying ?

I mean to say that the manufacture of this process butter may, for the moment, overcome certain flavours, tastes and qualities ; but I say also that by the process of boiling- as the hon. gentleman described it, melting is really the term-the quality of the butter is destroyed, and though it is afterwards chilled and put upon the market, there is only one way by which it can be done properly or successfully. That way is to incorporate in the butter a certain quantity of milk in which it is washed. That milk immediately deteriorates, and the butter will not keep and cannot be put upon the market with a good reputation. The statement that this butter can be kept ad infinitum is not correct. In some instances, it may have been frozen and kept in that condition, for a time. I believe it has been. But the statements that it is kept for a length of time can only be based upon the keeping of the butter by freezing, which is impracticable for the ordinary trade of the country. As a matter of fact, the experience of the United States has shown that butter cannot be kept under ordinary circumstances and retain its flavour and condition. At the same time, it may be sold by the manufacturer so as to get it on the market,

and be made, for tbe time being, to appear to be a reasonably good article of food.
I do not wish to interrupt the hon. minister, but X would like to ask him what he means by the word ' manufacturer '-would that include the farmer who makes the butter ?
Yes, it is provided in the Bill that the word ' manufacturer ' applies to any body making butter.
The hon. gentleman's amendment reads ' manufacturer or exporter ' and I thought perhaps it would not apply to the farmer who made the butter.

It would. The clause under discussion at the moment, which deals with the sixteen per cent of water, would apply to any body in the country. I think I explained that pretty thoroughly when the Bill was under discussion before.
I was not present.

As to this matter of process butter, and dealing with what my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), has said, I cannot help reiterating most emphatically-and I take the full responsibility of doing so here as Minister of Agriculture, and as having studied this question from its very base up -that it is absolutely necessary in the interest of the dairy trade in Canada that we should to-day put a stop to the manufacture of process butter in this country. My hon. friend speaks of this firm in Winnipeg. They have written to. me, and in their letter to me they stated that the present laws of the United States were pernicious, and that those laws dealt with people who were engaged in the manufacture of this article in a way unjust and unfair. I want my hon. friend to understand that in the United States these laws were passed by congress a year or a year and a half ago, because they found that the manufacture of process butter in the United States was bringing the butter trade in their country into an intolerable impasse. And they went only so far as to restrict and license it, because the manufacture has reached such a point of vested rights that they were not able to do what we are proposing to do today, and what they would have been glad to do could they have done it. And it is because these restrictive laws have been passed in the United States that these people interested in the manufacture of process butter are trying to establish their trade in Canada, a trade which has hurt the dairy trade of the United States and that would have the same results here. I take the full responsibility of saying this, and I throw upon any person who trys to prevent the prohibition of process butter in Canada the
responsibility of a disastrous injury to our butter trade.

I fear that the hon. Minister of Agriculture is going altogether too far in the amendment which he has just proposed. It seems to me that we are over careful in the restrictions that we are placing upon ordinary trade. I am not making any reference to process butter, something which I know very little about, and consequently will not speak of. But I think it a very dangerous thing to place a penalty upon a man who chances to blij butter, and with the making of which he had nothing to do, simply because it lias in it a certain proportion of water. The hon. minister tells us that ordinary butter contains about 13 per cent of water. Now there is very little difference between 13 per cent and 1G per cent, so little that a merchant dealing in butter might easily have in his possession at any time butter that actually contains 16 per cent. I think that these restrictions thrown around the butter trade are quite uncalled for, and they are dangerous, for they are liable to get a man into trouble at almost any time quite unwittingly. More latitude should be given. In fact, I believe the people have been getting along very well by making their own rules and regulations in regard to dairy butter, and I fear the minister is not going to benefit the ordinary people of the country by such restrictions as he proposes.

The amendment I now propose does not in any way extend the provisions of this Bill as they were passed after discussion by this committee. This proposed change is simply a. change in form ; it does not add to the restriction agreed to by this committee a little while ago.

I would ask the minister if. after having brought this Bill to this stage, he would not consider the matter of letting it rest until next year. I know there are many farmers in the west who have come in without means and who have accumulated three of four cows, and if this Bill is passed, it will deprive them of the means of making a living. Let the Bill stand over so as to give them a warning, that they may take steps to establish creameries. I know plenty of families who have come in there and who get their entire living, with what they make on the railways, out of three or four cows, because they do not patronize the creameries. I do not think it will endanger the country in any way to delay the passing of this Bill. There are many men coming in from Austria, Iceland and from Finland who depend upon three or four cows to make a living for the first two or three years, and if these people are not allowed to sell their butter except at three cents a pound, they will simply be compelled to give up making

butter to sell. I do not think it will do any harm to hold the Bill over for one year so that the government may take steps to come to their rescue and establish creameries in Manitoba under the supervision of the government, the same as they have done in the Territories.

I have pointed out already my reasons for not delaying the Bill. If we delay the Bill, vested interests will spring up in the country which will make it more difficult to pass such a law as this. My hon. friend speaks about the poor settlers in Manitoba. Though there may be a few who do not make butter good enough to sell for more than three or four cents a pound, I know that there are in Manitoba a number of successful creameries, as well as in the other provinces, where the people make a quality of butter which is much better than that my hon. friend describes. If these people are making butter which is only worth three or four cents in the market, they will not get more than three or four cents from the manufacturers mentioned. These will get the butter for the least possible price and the profits will go to the firm in Winnipeg who are making this process butter, and not the farmers.

I understand the minister is not making any material alteration in the provisions of section 4 by his amendment, he is merely changing the wording. But I understood him to say that it is possible to make butter with over Hi per cent water in it. Now supposing a farmer's wife should bring a roll of butter into a country store which contained 16 per cent of water or over, how is the purchaser to know that it does contain that quantity of water ? It is impossible for him to know, yet the moment he purchases that butter he is liable to a heavy penalty. To my mind the effect of this legislation will be that people dealing in this article will simply have to tell the farmers that they must pay them one or two cents a pound less in order to protect themselves. I believe this legislation is altogether against the interests of the farmers of the country.

It would be a disaster if a great national industry of this country was to be made subservient to a few people who are producing an article of butter not fit to eat, and certainly not fit to be exported. The people in England are turning towards this country at the present time for their food supply, and it is for our food supply we are endeavouring to get a reputation in England. I think tile objection of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) will be done away with very shortly, because there are no people who so quickly get down to making a good article of butter as our Canadian farmers. I am not at all afraid that there will be much injury done to the butter trade by
Mr. McCreary.
passing the Bill now before us. I would not delay it for a year, because it is highly important at the present time that everything that can be done to give this country a good standing in the markets of England and of Europe should be done at once.
'The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. When the Bill was passing through committee at a previous stage there was a discussion on clause 10 which describes the penalty, and my attention was drawn to the fact that the penalties ranging from .8100 down to $10 were not sufficiently restricted. There are two classes of offences under this Act, one being the manufacture of these forbidden articles, and then there are several other clauses defining smaller offences. I wish to divide the penalties into two classes ; therefore, instead of clause 10, I wish to substitute the following :
Every person who, by himself or through the agency of another person, violates any of the provisions of this Act, shall, for each offence, upon summary conviction, he liable to a fine not exceeding $50 and not less than $10 for such offence in violation of any of the provisions of sections 4. 8 and 9 of this Act ; and not exceeding $400 and not less than $200 if such offence be a violation of any of the provisions of sections 5, 6 or 7 of this Act, together with the costs of prosecution, and in default of payment of such fine and costs, shall be liable to imprisonment, with or without hard labour, for a term not exceeding three months unless such fine and the costs of enforcing it are sooner paid.
Amendment agreed to.

There was a little discussion the other day upon the question of local trade where small packages of butter are marked ' creamery.' I did not consider that this amounted to a great deal, and I was very anxious that the general provisions of the Act should apply specially to the export trade. Since then, various representations have reached me showing that there is in Ontario especially, a considerable trade in rolls and prints and small packages which are marked for local trade ' creamery.' Now, these are packages which cannot be used for export, therefore putting the word 'creamery' on them does not injure in any way our export trade. As my object in providing that the word ' creamery ' should not be put upon packages of butter, was for the purpose of protecting our export trade, I propose to add as section 16 of the Act the following :
Nothing contained in sections eight and nine of this Act shall apply to butter in rolls, prints or packages of less than twenty-five pounds in weight, not intended for export.
I think that will permit this local trade, which I have described a few minutes ago, still to employ the word ' creamery,' without injuring our export trade.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. What about the butter put up in tins ?

The words used are ' rolls, prints or packages of less than 25 pounds in weight.' Packages for export never include less than 25 pounds. I have made inquiries of my officers, and they tell me that they have not seen for years a package of less than 25 pounds sent for export. The ordinary packages are 50 pounds, and in some cases half that amount.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. But butter is frequently put up in tins of from two to five pounds each.
That would not come under this clause, these packages would come under the ordinary provisions of the Act.
That would not hinder a man shipping in boxes a large number of these pound packages of butter.
No, but he could not put the word ' creamery ' on them.

In the county which I represent we have a number of farmers who supply Toronto restaurants with butter. 'They send it into the city in packages containing fifty pounds and some as much as seventy-five pounds, sending it by express instead of driving it in by wagon. That section would prohibit them from stamping their butter as creamery butter for the reason that they send it by express from their station to Toronto in boxes containing more than twenty-five pounds. May I ask the hon. minister if the section would apply -to butter sold in this way ?

Not if it were in rolls, or prints, or blocks. If each package was done up in paper marked ' creamery ' then it would come in under this proviso and it would not be subject to the penalty for putting ' creamery ' upon it, although they might send it in boxes full of these prints.
If they put fifty one pound packages in a box and send it by express to Toronto they would not come under the penalty of this Bill ?

No.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 208) to amend the Post Office Act.-The Postmaster General.

Would the lion. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Muloek) explain how this affects the present law ?

Under the present law there are four classes. Hon. gentlemen will perhaps remember that last year we created a fourth class with salaries ranging from $400 to $600. That left a class from $600 to $800 and another class from $S00 to $1,200. To-day, instead of having the fourth class with a maximum of $600 we propose to make the maximum $700 so that the salaries will run from $400 to $700. Then, we come to the third class. The third class is divided into two grades, the junior third class from $700 to $800 and a senior third class from $800 to $900. Instead of stopping at $800 as the maximum, it will now be possible by getting into the senior division of the third class to get a maximum of $900. Then, instead of as at present, the first-class commencing at $800 and going up to $1,200, there are two second-class subdivisions, a junior second beginning at
