speechtext: 8900 and going up to 81-000 and a senior second beginning at 81-000 and going up to 81,200.
In the second-class they can go np to 81,200, can they not ?

In the third class they go from $700 to 8900, in the second class from $900 to SI .200, and in the first class from $1,200 to $1,500. I leave the first class the same as before-from $1,200 to $1,500. There are three classes prior to getting to the first class.
You are only dividing them up without increasing the maximum ?

I am not increasing the maximum. You might be willing to give a man $1,000 a year whom you would not be willing to give $1,200. You might want to promote a man from $800 to $1,000 and by putting him into the third class, by gradual increases he might go up to $1,000, but you do not wish to be compelled to put him into a class in which he might reach a higher maximum than he was worth.
Have you figured up the amount by which this will increase the expenditure in your department ?

It will amount to a very considerable increase, I think. I will give that in the estimates. It will be in the supplementary estimates which are already prepared to be submitted to the House in anticipation of these amendments. Speaking from memory-perhaps I am in error-I think that these various increases will involve an increase in the expenditure of from $30,000 to $40,000 a year.
I think so, but I would not like to be held by these figures.
If you transfer a person from the inside service to the outside service, the law provides that he will be required to pass an examination, but you abolish that under this Bill ?

At present there are promotion examinations under the Civil Service Act. but these promotion examinations have no specific reference to the duties of the office. It appears to me, when it comes to promotion, that the examination should not be on the work learned at schools but on the work learned in the department. After a young man has passed his civil service qualifying examination, and years go by, if he is deserving of promotion, I do not think it is fair to ask him to go back to the class of work involved in text books. The proper subject of examination is in reference to the duties of his office.
You will require a grade or class examination ?

The department will prescribe the examination having reference to the work on which the man is engaged. If he were a railway mail clerk we would want one kind of examination, and if a clerk in the department, a different examination.
I understand, but under this Bill you abolish the examination ?
Only the promotion examination.

You abolish any examination. Subsection 4 says :
Without being required to pass any examination except-
I see that section provides for such an examination as may be prescribed under regulations to be passed by the Postmaster General.

Yes, such an examination as we prescribe. The principle of these changes is the same principle sis is applied in the case of railway mail clerks. tinder the former law iiie inspectors were appointed at an initial salary which they remained at for ten years and jumped pt once from that figure ti another, and after remaining for a further ten years they were eligible for promotion to a no,-, her salaw they havin' served twenty years in all. I propose to apply the ordinary principle and let the salaries be increased by annual increments towards the maximum.
Hon. Mr. HAGGaRT. Would the annual increment amount at the end of ten years to more than the present system ?

I think not. Of course they would go step by step each year and would earn more in the ten years.
On section 8-salary of superintendent.
The maximum salary of superintendents is $l,5i'0 and it is proposed to make it $1,800.
How many superintendents have you ?

There is one superintendent for each railway mail division ; ten altogether, I think.
On section 9-newspaper postage.
How will this change in the newspaper postage rate aTeet the revenue ?

The object of this clause is to reduce the postage on newspapers carried within a limited zone of 300 miles. At present the rate is half a

cent a pound and we propose to reduce it to a quarter of a cent when the distance ol' transmission does not exceed 300 miles. The loss of revenue would probably amount to from $50,000 to $75,000 a year.
How will you discriminate in the case of papers to be delivered in places where there is a free delivery.

Suppose a publisher in Montreal desires to send ids papers to Ottawa where there is a free delivery he would pay the old rate. There is no difficulty about the arrangement. The publisher will separate them and we have officers to cheek them.
Will this new rate cover the cost ?
No.
The Postmaster General is a convert to this idea because X concurred in his opinion of some years ago that these newspapers should pay enough postage to recoup the country for the expense.

It seems to me that this is discriminating against enterprising journals whose circulation roaches out beyond 300 miles. Certainly some of these papers are among the very best publications we have, and they ought to be encouraged whereas by this law they have to pay half a cent a pound, and the others only one-quarter cent a pound. Take tiie ' Farmers Advocate ' for instance, which is an excellent journal, and which circulates from one end of the Dominion to the other, and it will be placed at a disadvantage by this postal rate. The ' Montreal Star ' is a newspaper that is subscribed f< r over the whole Dominion and a large proportion of its list of subscribers live more than 300 miles away from the place of publication. The ' Montreal Star ' would be at a like disadvantage. I cannot see the justice of this.

I think that this is a reform in the wrong direction. The Postmaster General is very well aware that there are valuable periodicals published in Canada which find their circulation at a greater distance than 300 miles from the otiice of issue. My hon. friend (Mr. Smith) has referred to the ' Farmers' Advocate.' That journal is circulated throughout the length and breadth of this country among the agricultural community and it is a very valuable paper. The postage should be reduced on.it rather than increased. I have a letter here which was sent me in the interests of the ' Farmers' Advocate ', and I am sure that when the Postmaster General, as he usually does, gives consideration to this matter in the interests of the farmers, he will come to the conclusion that the proposal in this Bill is a mistake. There are 184
other valuable publications in Canada which the farmers get a great deal of information from, and as we all know their circulation is mostly at a greater distance that 300 miles from the office of publication.

I hardly see how this can be regarded as an increase, and my hon. friend can hardly understand the proposed amendment. It is purely a reduction. If the press of Canada prefer the law to remain as it is, I would be more pleased than they. At present newspapers pay a rate of half a cent a pound, and I am reducing that to a quarter of a cent when the distance is not too great. Newspapers cannot be treated the same as letters. They are rather commercial goods delivered to us by the hundreds of tons, and I am not aware of any business principle which would warrant your carrying a ton of merchandise 3,000 miles at the same rate as 300 miles. It is not practicable to divide the whole Dominion into zones and charge by the distance carried, as is done by railways and express companies. However, if my hon. friend and the press prefer to have the law remain as it is, I shall be more than pleased.
Some prefer it and others do not.

There are none who prefer it in their hearts. It will he some time before this Bill can become law, as it has to pass the Senate, and there will be ample opportunity for the press to object to the measure. If they prefer to pay half a cent per pound in a zone of 100 miles, there will be no objection on my part.
This publisher prefers it.
He really does not.
Have you calculated the loss ?
From $50,000 to $75,000 a year. This is substantially a reduction of $50,000 to $75,000 to the press.

I understand that it is a reduction, but at the same time it discriminates against certain publications. It discriminates against periodical or agricultural newspapers, such as the ' Farmers' Advocate.' The newspapers are issued daily and have a circulation within much less than 300 miles, but publications such as the ' Farmers' Advocate ' are circulated east and west and north and south throughout the whole country, and the greatest portion of their circulation is outside the 300-mile limit. Therefore these publishers would prefer the rates left as they are. Here is what the publishers of the ' Farmers' Advocate ' write :



We see that the government has brought In a Bill to amend the Post Office Act which contains a proviso reducing the rate on newspapers from one-half cent to one-quarter cent per pound for a radius of 300 miles. We -desire to point out that the 300 mile radius is very unfair to many publishers including ourselves. Publications that can command an extensive circulation outside of the 300 mile zone must necessarily have merits and are of more importance to our country than those of a restricted circulation, and instead of the rate of postage being increased beyond the 300 miles, it would be more in the interest of this country to give such papers a lower rate. We would prefer to see the half-cent per pound remain as it is or even increase the rate and put every paper in the country on the same basis doing away with the present free postage for 20 mile zone. Otherwise allow all papers free postage as formerly. The proposed change will discriminate against the ' Farmers Advo-vate ' as much, if not more than any other paper in Canada, as more than half its circulation is beyond the 300 mile limit.

I would like to offer my congratulations to the hon. the Postmaster General for his efforts on behalf of the outside service. It seems to me a step in the right direction for the civil service generally to have the position of these gentlemen a little improved. If there is any class of men in the service underpaid, it certainly Is the outside service, such as the letter carriers and the clerks in the city offices. At the same time I would ask the hon. gentleman to endeavour to take the whole question of salaries into consideration. Thirty years ago, when the maximum was fixed, it was a pretty fair rate, but to-day it is too small. In the city of Ottawa everything has gone up In price. Rents have increased and the prices of ail commodities, so that $1,000 to-day is not as good as $600 was a few years ago. If the hon. gentleman would use his influence and continue the work begun in his own department and use his influence with members of the other departments, he would be entitled to the gratitude of the civil service. Three years ago, without any compulsion, we advanced our own indemnity. If we can do that for ourselves, we ought to be able to do as much for others and give them good value for their services.

We have drifted
away from the question of newspaper postage. Can the hon. minister tell us the amount of money realized on newspaper postage during the last year ?
Something over $100,000, probably $125,000.

It is proposed to
make a change in the law, in which I agree in some respects, though perhaps uot in all, because I think it involves considerable discrimination. It is proposed to reduce the postage on newspapers to a gross amount estimated at from $50,000 to $75,000 a year, so that practically all the revenue that the

hon. gentleman will get from newspaper postage will be $25,000 or $30,000. It seems to me that the enormous amount of labour keeping track of this postage) will eat up all tlie revenue, and I think the hon. gentleman would do very well to go back to the good old days when knowledge was not taxed in this way and newspapers were sent all over the country free. The hon. gentleman says he has a surplus. I do not fear that this will wipe out the surplus, but I think It is hardly worth while charging a postage on newspapers, from which we obtain but $25,000 to $30,000 a year, and which is paid by certain sections of the country. There is no doubt that some classes of newspapers will receive more favourable consideration under this change. Take the province of Quebec for instance, as a rule tlie newspapers of that province do not circulate outside its limits. The 300-mile limit, I take it means a distance of 000 miles from end to end. This would practically cover the whole province of Quebec. Therefore, the newspapers published in French, with rare exceptions, would pay but little postage, while the newspapers published in Montreal in English and circulating over the Dominion, such as the Montreal ' Star,' will be called upon to pay a considerable amount in postage. I simply use this to show that there is a discrimination. I do not think that the Postmaster General's object in changing the law is to give a special benefit to a particular class, but it works out in that way. And I think that rather than have it said that there is discrimination, it would be better to do aw-ay with postage on newspapers altogether.
How much revenue would be derived from the newspapers outside the 300-mile zone ?

My recollection is that the postal revenue from newspapers is from $125,000 to $150,000. My deputy advises me, from memory, that it is a little oveT $100,000, but I believe my recollection is a little more accurate. When I was asked what a loss this would mean, I said it would be about half the revenue, for I presume that half of the newspapers are within the 300-mile limit. It Is probable that after this Bill becomes law, if it does become law, we shall collect somewhere in the neighbourhood of $75,000 a year for postage on newspapers.

I do not often ask the government to take my view of a case, but I would urge upon the Postmaster General to withdraw the discrimination he proposes upon one class of newspapers. I am in favour of a reduction in postage, but I cannot understand why this discrimination takes place. I know that the Postmaster General represents an agricultural constituency and is interested in a farming community.

Why he should put an extra tax on published periodicals, while allowing political sheets to be sent about at about half the rate, I cannot understand. All those who subscribe to the [DOT] Farmers' Advocate ' and all other periodicals which circulate throughout the length and breadth of this co'unrry ought not to be subject to this tax. I hope the hon. Postmaster General will reconsider the matter and place all these publications on the same basis.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cargill) speaks of discrimination, but he has not brought forward any argument toj prove that discrimination is proposed. At present there is a uniform rate for all Canada of half a cent a pound, regardless of the distance, as there is a uniform rate for letters. But letters are posted separately, and it is absolutely impossible to vary the rate with the distance. But newspapers are posted by the car-load, just as the hon. member for East Bruce (Mr. Cargill) ships lumber. Would the hon. gentlemen think it discrimination to have a certain rate on lumber from his mill to Toronto, and a different rate from his mill to a point at double the distance ? If not, the same argument will apply to newspapers. I am in favour of uniformity in the benefits and burdens of legislation. I do not believe hi discrimination of any kind, but hold that all should be equal before the law and all interests should be treated alike by the law. If every newspaper in Canada should pay a quarter of a cent per pound for transmission of papers for a certain district, all are treated alike. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) speaks of newspapers in Quebec. Well, take Toronto which is one of the great centres of newspaper publication, many newspapers published in Toronto are transmitted for a greater distance than 300 miles. No matter where the newspaper is, it will get the benefit of the reduction. The only discrimination that I can see in the matter is the discrimination in favour of the press in giving them transmission of goods at lower rates than are given, other people by railway. That is class legislation, I admit. If we desire to do away witli discrimination. the right direction in which to move would be in the direction of increase in postage on newspapers.

I am sorry that the hon. Postmaster General cannot see that he is discriminating against some publications in favour of others. * For instance, he is supposed to be) the proprietor of a newspaper in Toronto called the Toronto ' Star.'
I wish I was.

The circulation of that newspaper, I feel sure is confined within a radius of one hundred miles. So the hon. gentleman circulates that paper at a cost 184}
of one-quarter cent per pound. But if 1 were the publisher of the * Farmers' Advocate ' in Toronto and the large bulk of my subscribers lived in the maritime provinces or Manitoba or the North-west Territories, my Bill for postage would be very heavy. This appears to me to be a clear discrimination against newspapers of wide circulation.

I ask leave to make just one observation in answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cargill). Of course, he has no authority or foundation for the suggestion he made as to my being the proprietor of the Toronto ' Star ' or any other newspaper. I wish I were the proprietor of the ' Star,' for it is a very valuable educational journal, if I may be permitted to say so. I have been credited with being the owner of a number of newspapers, but I am not. I am not the owner of the ' Star,' and have no more interest in it than my hon. friend (Mr. Cargill), except, perhaps, that I am a better well-wisher of it than lie is.
I have no objection to the ' Star ' at all.

Before the Bill is reported, I would ask the Postmaster General if he has considered the advisability of incorporating a section in the Bill, on the lines suggested by me, to make an allowance to mail clerks for detention. I pointed out that trains are often storm-bound or otherwise delayed, and mail clerks are kept for hours in employment for which time they receive no remuneration. Then they often have to purchase one or two meals and, in the west these cost something-fifty to seventy-five cents each. Yet the mail clerks receive no allowance for this, nor any remuneration for the extra hours they serve. I suggested an allowance of twenty-five cents per hour for this detention. I mention the matter again because, as I understand it, if the Bill is reported without the clause to the effect I suggest, the Postmaster General may not be in a position to make an allowance of that kind.

The hon. member for Yale and Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) mentioned this matter at an earlier stage of the Bill. I think there is much in the point he has mentioned. But whether it can be satisfactorily arranged at this period of the session I do not know. I have handed the ' Hansard ' containing his remarks to the officers of the department, to see if it is possible to devise a practical scheme to give effect to the hon. gentleman's wishes. However, it will not be necessary to have such a provision by statute. It can be provided for by an item in the estimates, just as, to-day, we have items making provisional allowance for the west where the conditions are different from those of the east.

I wish to say that I was in error in what I said a moment ago.
I was under the impression that the Postmaster General was simply extending the 20-mile limit to a 300-mile limit. I And he is making three zones instead of two. However, it does not materially alter my argument with regard to discrimination. I was in error when I stated that in the province of Quebec, French daily newspapers would be carried free, whereas English papers that would extend throughout the Dominion would have to pay half a cent a pound. I should have said the French papers w;ould pay one-quarter of a cent per pound.

There are a couple of points I would like to bring to the attention of the Postmaster General. For months past, I am informed, the mail cars supplied in the western part of this country have not furnished sufficient space for the mail clerks. In several instances, when the mail is of an excessive quantity, it has to be put in box cars, and this greatly hampers the work of the mail clerks. Another point is that under the regulations, so I am informed, a mail car requires to be placed in a certain part of the train, in a certain position with regard to the engine, and that this regulation is being often broken. I desire to call these points to the attention of the Postmaster General.

I would ask the minister if he has given any further attention to the question of the increase of pay for country postmasters ? I think this subject has been brought to his attention several times in the past. We have a large number of postmasters in country districts who are receiving salaries of from $10 up to .$30 or $40. In my county there are some places where the country merchant at the cross roads, who has kept a post office for several years, has now refused to continue that post office, and in some cases the office has been removed from the store and given to the blacksmith : this is not very satisfactory. I think a clause should be introduced into this Bill to make provisions for these salaries. I am not asking that increases should be given in all places, but there is certainly no comparison between the present pay of the officers referred to in the Bill and the pay received by country postmasters generally. The minister. of course, will reply that the revenue in these country offices is very small. That is quite true, but that is caused by the system of centralization. A large number of people who used to receive their mail matter in the rural districts are now receiving it at the town where they have to go frequently for business. In the province of Ontario, farmers who are directing their attention to making butter and cheese and raising poultry require to go to the post office more frequently than formerly to attend to correspondence or to watch the market. I am of the opinion that some arrangement should

be made whereby country postmasters would receive a reasonable allowance to which they are entitled. I wish to direct the minister's attention to another matter, and that is the very small pay that is received by the mail carrier^ in country districts. Some of them drive six or eight miles for the small sum of fifty cents.
Are these not contracts given out by tender ?

Sometimes they are, and sometimes they are not. Perhaps they do not do it that way in the hon. gentleman's riding, but in many cases these engagements are made without tender. I am not complaining of that principle, but I say that some rearrangement of the routes should be made in the country districts, so that the mail carriers could receive a proper remuneration.
I brought this matter to the attention of the Postmaster General a few evenings ago.

Would the hon. gentleman permit me to make an observation ? The salaries of the postmasters are not determined by statute, except it be the salaries of city postmasters, but they are determined by the Postmaster General. The statute gives that power to him, therefore no legislation is necessary. In a little while the estimates of the Postmaster General will be before the House, and I think that would be a more appropriate time to discuss these matters that are foreign to this Bill. I have no doubt that this whole subject of salaries to postmasters will then come up for consideration.

I am glad to hear the Postmaster General make that announcement, and knowing the generous heart which he possesses, I hope he will pay some attention to the requests we have made on behalf of the country pcstmasters.

Before the Bill is finally adopted, I wish to express my hearty approval of it, and at the same time to express the gratitude of the civil servants, who are receiving at the hands of the Postmaster General substantial justice in the increase of salary which he has provided for them. I had hoped that another portion of the service under the control of the Postmaster General would also receive by this Bill the increase to which they are entitled. I refer more particularly to a number of temporary employees, of whom there are a large number in Ottawa, whose position is rather unsatisfactory, in that it is temporary. There are civil servants who have been in the employ of the various departments for many years, and whose employment is still of a temporary character. They also. I think, are deserving of an increase which, under the law as it now stands, it is not found possible to give

them. I hope that before the session closes, or at all events early next session, the temporary employees of the Post Office and other" Departments, whose position, as I say, is unsatisfactory on account of the nature of their tenure of office, and because of the insufficient salary which is paid them, will receive the government's attention. I am sure that if the Hon. Postmaster General comes to their relief he will be entitled to the gratitude of that class of civil servants, just as he is now entitled to receive gratitude at the hands of those who are employed in the outside service and who are provided for in this Bill. I do not know if he lias considered the matter, or if lie is in a position to tell us what, if any, measure of relief he is prepared to grant to this class.

This Bill is limited entirely to the post office clerks. My hon. friend refers to another class in the service, a temporary class which is scattered through all the departments. It would not be appropriate, therefore, that a Bill dealing solely with one department should deal with a class of temporary employees found in all the departments. Legislation with reference to the civil service is done by amendments to the Civil Service Act, and it has generally devolved upon the Minister of Finance to take charge of legislation of that character.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. While on this subject, I would ask the Postmaster General whether he has given attention to the need of reorganizing the staff of the Winnipeg post office ? The staff there is quite inadequate, and the salaries paid so far have been so low that the government have not been able to secure the services of qualified men. Last year I moved for a return of the number of employees who have been engaged in the Winnipeg post office for a few years, both permanent and temporary, and I was furnished with a list of over 300 names, showing that men were actually coming in and going out from that office after a short time, both on account of inefficiency, and more especially on account of the small salary they were getting, because they could do far better by leaving the post office and getting employment elsewhere. We cannot get a permanent staff of officials for that office for the paltry salaries that are being paid so far. This Bill will provide for an increase in the salaries of post office clerks, and also for the selection of better qualified officers. I believe that the number of officers emploved in the Winnipeg post office is quite inadequate for the services required.

I do not thiuk that the Winnipeg post office is suffering from an insufficiency of staff. The Winnipeg post office is suffering from several causes, one the inadequacy of the accommodation. The city is extremely prosperous, it is growing and there has been a growing congestion in the government building in
Winnipeg. The government building at Winnipeg is used not only for post office purposes but for the purposes of the customs house and Inland Revenue Department, and with the increased activity in Winnipeg and the west, lack of accommodation makes it very difficult to handle the business satisfactorily. In addition to that circumstance we have had a great transition in Winnipeg, as it has grown from what it was a few years ago until it is now a leading metropolitan city. That in itself seems to require a staff different from what was formerly required. Again, the former postmaster has been recently superannuated. He had been in office many years. He was a most faithful man, but he was advanced in years. He had had no post office experience and he had not educated up under him a staff equal to the growing requirements of the city. The assistant postmaster had for many years been an invalid, a paralytic, and my bon. friend (Mr. La-Riviere) is aware how great the consideration is which is usually extended to a public officer under these circumstances. I found him in that condition and I leaned the side of leniency and consideration towards him. The staff reported that they could get along very well and he was allowed to remain in office filling a responsible position, the duties of which he was not able properly to discharge. The postmaster himself was gradually becoming unfit for duty, and there was no efficient staff growing up to take charge * of the growing business of the Winnipeg post office. Well, the process of improvement cannot take place with the stroke of the pen. There must be a gradual education.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. How long is it since the present postmaster was appointed to office ?

Not two years ago. The late postmaster was superannuated. the assistant postmaster paralyzed and ultimately dying, and now we are having practically new officers. The new postmaster is getting into his business and beginning to learn it. He is a good business man, I think my hon. friend will admit, a man who is considered fully qualified, as far as business attainments are concerned, for the office; and with experience, I have no doubt will fully justify his appointment. However, it takes a little time for a man to get into the work. We have some good officers there. We are endeavouring under the system now in force to educate men in the technical work of the post office at the best offices and have them available to be despatched to other offices to educate the staffs there. We have in the last few months sent to the Winnipeg post office three expert post office men. They will be of great service in educating the rest of the staff and bringing them up to a proper de-
[DOT] 5867

gi'ee of efficiency, and I think if we could only get more accommodation everything would be satisfactory there. At present you cannot find an idle building in Winnipeg. There is a large amount of mail matter arriving in Winnipeg for transmission beyond that has to stay over for other trains, and yet, at the present time, there is no way of handling that mail matter except by taking it to the city post office. There is no accommodation in the station and there is no building near the station to be rented. The Canadian Pacific Railway are erecting a new station and in that new station they will provide ample accommodation for the post office so that mail matter not required locally will be handled at the station. At present there is no way of doing that and it has to be taken to the city post office. Hon. gentlemen can see that this is a waste of money and produces a state of congestion in the post office itself. Unless the Canadian Pacific Railway satisfy us that they are going on with proper despatch to have that building erected the government will be obliged to erect a building at the station so as to avoid having to dump into the Winnipeg post office mail matter that is not required for delivery in the city of Winnipeg. But, in the meantime, I can assure my hon. friend that the standard of efficiency of the Winnipeg post office is rapidly being improved and that the trouble has not been because of an insufficiency of officers but because of an insufficiency of accommodation. I think I am correct in saying that the report recently showed that the number of officers there was more than was required, but the drawback there is because of the difficulty in getting good results out of them.

speechtext: House proceeded to consider amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 82) respecting and restricting Chinese Immigration.-The Prime Minister.

These amendments are two in number. The first provides that a Chinaman shall not be subjected to the tax when he is the personal attendant or servant of a British subject visiting Canada. The tax is collectable but can be refunded to him. The section reads as follows :
In the ease of a person of Chinese origin, who is a personal attendant of or servant of a British subject visiting Canada, the tax payable under the first subsection of section six may be refunded to the person paying the same, upon his furnishing satisfactory evidence that such Chinese attendant or servant is leaving the port of entry with his employer or master on his return to China, if within twelve months of the date of his arrival in Canada and upon returning to the controller of such port the certificate granted under section thirteen.
The second amendment is to provide that Chinamen employed upon the steamers, which ply on the Pacific ocean, may land and do their work without paying the tax.

speechtext: Bill (No. 204) to amend Acts relating to Naturalization and Aliens.-The Prime Minister) read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon.

The object of this Bill is simply to amend one or two clauses bf the Naturalization Act in order to facilitate the

proceedings whereby naturalization can be obtained by aliens. The hon. member for Frovencher has suggested that a change is necessary in Manitoba and I propose to make the following change :
Such certificate shall be presented in Manitoba to the court of King's Bench during its sittings in the judicial district in which the alien resides, or, if the alien resides in the eastern judicial district, to a judge of the court of King's Bench sitting in court or to the court of assize and nisi prius, during its sittings in the judicial district in which the alien resides, or to the county court of the county court division within which the alien resides.
With regard to the North-west Territories, I propose to strike out the clause and substitute the following :
In the North-west Territories to a judge of the Supreme Court of the North-west, sitting in chambers in the judicial district within which the alien resides.
It is more convenient to make the application to the judge in chambers than to the court.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. H n. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: But the general principle is that the naturalization of an alien shall be in open court.
By a subsequent section we provide that notice shall be given of any application to be naturalized. As the law now stands, no notice is required.

Amendments agreed to.
On section 2,

The amendment you have just made, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the application to judge iu the North-west Territories, will necessitate an amendment here also, because this clause provides only for sittings in court. Therefore, I propose the following as subsection 5 :
In the North-west Territories the foregoing provisions of this section shall not apply, but in lieu thereof the procedure shall be as follows :-
On the presentation of the certificate, the judge shall cause a copy thereof to be posted up in a conspicious place in the court-house in which he holds his chambers for at least two weeks.
At any time after the said copy is so posted any one may file with the clerk of the court where the said copy has been posted a written notice of objection to the certificate of naturalization being granted, stating the grounds of such objection. On the Wednesday following the expiration of the two weeks for which the copy is required to be posted, the judge shall hold a sittings in chambers, at which, if no ob, jection_has been raised, he shall direct the issue of a certificate of naturalization to the applicant, and if objection has been raised he shall decide such objection in a summary way. The judge shall have power to adjourn the said hearing from time to time.
Amendment agreed to.
I would ask the Prime Minister if any provision is to be made with reference to repatriated Canadians ?
We are just coming to that.

I was called out of the House unexpectedly to the telephone a moment ago, and did not hear the explanation with regard to section 2. I do not understand why the Prime Minister is making it necessary to put in this notice. With the indulgence of the committee. I would like to hear an explanation. I presume that section 11 applies to the whole Dominion.

speechtext: We are still on section 2. Of course, we have just considered the addition of a subsection-subsection 5.
If necessary, I will move to reconsider.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not necessary.

We have not found any difficulty, so far as I know under the present system, and no frauds have been perpetrated. That system is that the applicant goes before the magistrate and proves his residence and other qualifications. The magistrate gives a certificate, and that is filed any day before the opening of the court. These applications are called at the opening of the court and again at the closing, which may be the day following or a week later. Of course, it may be the same day, but very rarely. Everybody who is interested has notice from the opening of the court of what is to be done, so that any attempted fraud may be checked. Under the system now proposed, a good deal more labour and trouble would be thrown upon the applicant. He has to give notice in writing, stating name, residence and occupation, and file it with the clerk of the court at least three weeks before the sitting. I fear that this will mean that people will be obliged to employ a solicitor or attorney to draw the notice and present it in due time. This will throw difficulties in the way of the naturalization of aliens, and this, I think, ought not to be done except for urgent reason. I would ask the Prime Minister what necessity has arisen for this change ?

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) that when this Bill was first discussed this subject struck me very much as it has struck him. I thought that the less formality there was

about au alien getting his naturalization papers the better it would be. In the old provinces, the law as it is has worked to the satisfaction of everybody. There has been no fraud complained of. But I understand that, in the North-west Territories, where immigrants are coming in in very large numbers, these formalities are necessary in order to prevent fraud. I agree with my hon. friend that it would have been better to afford facilities to an alien who wishes to become a British subject. At the same time, certain things must be complied with under the law. An alien in the Northwest must be a resident for a certain time before he can become a British subject. The law has placed it at three years. We are assured that unless we have some restriction, some notice given for the time provided in the Bill, it is possible that frauds will be committed-in fact frauds have been committed already. That is the only object of the ameudment.

I quite grasp what the Prime Minister has said-that it is necessary to make this provision because of the special conditions in the North-west Territories. But would he not consider the advisability of incorporating this in the amendment which provides special practice with regard to the North-west Territories and leave the general practice for the rest of Canada as it is ?

I would not give an answer off hand to my hon. friend on that subject. But if he will let the Bill go through, we will have the third reading delayed so that I may have an opportunity of discussing it.

I have had a little experience in the courts with respect to matters of this sort, and that experience leads me to believe that, while it is desirable to facilitate the naturalization of those who come to this country for the purpose of becoming citizens, it is also desirable to know something about the men who are to have the great advantage of becoming Canadian citizens. At the sittings of the court in the province of Quebec, for instance, the clerk gets up, and, in the hurry and jumble of the preliminary business, reads the list of names. Nobody knows what is going on, or is aware of who the applicants for naturalization are. I think the suggestion that three weeks notice should be given beforehand is not an undue burden to put upon a man who desires the great advantage of being naturalized as a Canadian citizen.

But the notice to be given as advocated by the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) does not draw the attention of anybody more than does the reading in the court. No one finds it out unless he is searching for it. But, under the present law, those who are in-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
teres ted in the matter know that the announcement is to be made at the opening of the court, and can search to see what the applications are.
But the publication of notice on the first day of the court is still required, while the posting up of notice for two weeks in advance is required in addition-it is an additional precaution.

I admit that, but the filing provided for by the Act we are now passing does not attract anyone's attention. No one will know by the filing of this notice who are entitled to be naturalized, unless his attention is drawn to it, and unless he is sufficiently interested to go and search.

The hon. gentleman from Lincoln and Niagara (Mr. Lancaster), mentioned the point about this applying exclusively to the North-west Territories. In British Columbia we are face to face with a very serious problem, and that is the naturalization of Japanese and Chinese. There was a case in Vancouver where some 1,100 Japanese were made British subjects, and I venture to say on my responsibility as a member of parliament that two-thirds cf these men had not been in the country for more than one year. The majority of the Japanese who come into our country have only been there about three years. As a matter of fact, these men are put through the mill, as you might say, far tco hurriedly. One man was found who so far forgot the oath of his office as to say that he was prepared, for fifty cents a piece, to put these men through their facings and make them British subjects. Of course we are all glad to see new citizens coming into our country. 1 think this law is an excellent law, and ought to apply to all parts of the Dominion. A man who is himself a British subject is the best judge of the men who are likely to make good British subjects, and we cannot hope to make out of these orientals anything like the British subjects that we would like to get. I hope the Prime Minister will appreciate the position we are placed in, and make the law applicable to British Columbia. The hon. gentleman suggested it should only apply to the North-west Territories.

I did not suggest that, but I was suggesting to the Prime Minister that as he admitted there was no trouble about the other provinces, he should make his section especially applicable to the North-west Territories.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 3,

I move to strike out this section. The law is made uniform now except in the district of Iveewatin

where the Governor in Council shall decide to whom application shall be made.
Section struck out.
On section 4,

I desire to call attention to section 18 of the Act which says :
A statutory alien may. upon the same terms and subject to the same conditions as are required in the case of an alien, apply for a certificate of naturalization.
And so on. A statutory alien is a British subject who has become the subject of another nation, and who wants to come back again to his British nationality. Therefore if Canadians who have gone to the States want to come back to Canada the law is that they must reside here three years in order to become British subjects again. We propose to [DOT] change that so that a residence of only three months will be sufficient.

I thought that under the British law no man could divest himself of his allegiance without the consent of his native country ; that although he had taken an oath of allegiance In a foreign country, as soon as he came back he continued to be a British subject, except in so far as his rights of naturalization in a foreign country were confirmed by treaty between that country and the imperial authorities. There is, then, a treaty existing between the United States and Great Britain by which British subjects can be naturalized in the United States ?

Yes. Now in consequence of this amendment it will be necessary to make another amendment. The statutory alien who wants to become a British subject will have to take an oath, the form of which is contained in the Act as form P. I therefore propose to amend form E in the schedule of the Naturalization Act by striking out the words ' has duly resided in Canada for a period of three years ' and substituting ' has duly resided in Canada for at least three months.'
Amendment agreed to.

Before the Bill is reported, I want to make an observation on a statement I understood the Prime Minister to make in the discussion of this Bill. He said that some irregularities had taken place in the North-west Territories, and that fraud had been committed. I want to say that so far as I know, and I am pretty well seized of the facts up there, I never heard any complaint of any fraud having been committed in the North-west Territories. I think it was in British Columbia in connection with the Japanese that frauds of that sort took place, but not in the Northwest Territories. The people of foreign
origin up there will not take it as a compliment to be told that they have tried to become naturalized before they had resided long enough in the country.

I apologize.
Bill reported.

speechtext: I would like to ask the right hon. minister if he could tell us something about the trade that is being done in South Africa.

speakername: The MINISTER QF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: Since the war is over ?

Yes, they have been well filled with cargo. What traffic we can obtain in return I am not prepared to say. Things are in a state of flux in South Africa

at the present time, and it is very hard to say what will develop there, but there is a great demand for certain articles which I think we can well jiroduce. For instance, we ought to he able to send a considerable quantity of lumber and large quantities of provisions. -Mr. WILSON. What do you expect by way of return freights ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
That is a point which we cannot well decide. There is not a very large quantity of articles raised in South Africa from which we can hope to secure return freights but we hope the trade will develop. speechtext:

Such articles as wool would come through London, because London is the great wool mart, and it is more convenient to import in that way. The House is aware that for several years back our sister colonies have been suffering from the most severe drought they have ever experienced, and our imports during the last few years cannot be taken as a fair indication, but in spite of everything our exports show on the whole a gratifying increase. Although Australia was at one time a wheat growing country, there has been found a very considerable demand for Canadian flour, and our agents report sales of Canadian flour at a very much higher rate than any other flour in the Australian market.

It is a matter for regret that this government does not establish direct steam communication between Canada and Australia, as we have done in the case of South Africa. It is impossible to carry on this trade successfully with the long railway haul from our manufacturing centres to the Pacific coast, and if we intend to compete with the American manufacturers, who have direct steamers from New York, then this government must establish steamers to run from Montreal and Quebec in summer, and from St. John and Halifax in winter direct to Australia.
Let me read this interview, with Mr. Bos-worth, one of the leading officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which bears on this subject:
Mr. Bosworth's attention was drawn to the statement made by Mr. John Gordon, the owner of large stores in Adelaide, Melbourne and Brisbane, of the possibility of opening up a considerable trade for Canadian cotton fabrics in Australia, but that he feared the charges entailed by the long railway haul over the prairies and through the mountains would prevent the development of such trade to very large dimensions.
Mr. Bosworth replied that the railway could not compete with ships running from eastern ports to Australia with cotton cargo, but a good beginning had already been made in the shipment of Canadian manufactured cotton to Australia. For some months past the Canadian Pacific has been carrying from 100 to 150 cases of cotton for Australia by each steamer.
This indicated that at existing rates a profitable market can be opened up for Canadian cotton in Australia. If the trade assumed such proportions as to warrant the running of vessels direct with Australia, the railway could not hope to successfully compete with ships, but there was no indication as yet that it would do so, although it was very encouraging to see its gradual growth.
Besides cheap woollen and cotton goods, we could export from Canada to Australia a large quantity of doors and sashes and dressed lumber if we had direct steamship communication. You can never have a successful Canadian industry unless you give facilities for export as well as for the home market. That is a thing that the manufacturers of Canada should see to at the earliest possible moment. What would England be to-day if her manufacturers were confined to supplying the home market ? I read recently that nearly three-quarters of the tonnage that passed through the Suez canal was of British ships, and that 75 per cent of the cargoes were from Great Britain. If we are going to follow in the wake of the great mother country, we must afford facilities to have our products carried to other markets than our own.

House again in committee on Bill (No. 176) to incorporate the Canadian Transportation and Storage Company.-Mr. German.
On section 7,	.

The general nature of this section is objectionable. It is recognized, as a general rule, that we should not give any company the power to acquire or purchase another company unless the latter be named. But here we have the power given *wholesale to this company to acquire others having the same object. That is against the prevailing idea of the present day that there should be no monopoly.

I do not see any objection to this company acquiring the rights of other companies having similar objects. Some other company may be in existence for the same purpose, and be not going on to do business at all.

I do not suppose there could be a monopoly by the combining of companies having dissimilar objects. A monopoly is a combination of companies having the same object, and it is one of the principles of our legislation to avoid that sort of thing. We find frequently the Railway Committee requiring a company applying for the power of amalgamation to name the companies with which it proposes to amalgamate.
There is only one company at present in existence-and I do not know that that has a legal existence at pre-

sent-which has the same objects as this one. That is the company which procured a-charter from this parliament, and which has in its act of incorporation a clause identical with this. I think that that com.-pany has become defunct through the lapse of tune, but there may be a company having similar objects which this company might desire to acquire. I cannot see any danger of monopoly. If another company desires to sell out, why should not this one acquire its rights ?

The government are responsible for all the legislation of this House, whether private or public, and the rule has always been strictly enforced that whenever any company wants to acquire the property and franchise of any other, it must name that other company which it proposes to buy. No one can tell what may lie the effect of a clause such as this.

This matter was considered by the committee, and a modification was made which it was thought would meet any fair ground for criticism. My hon. friend from Hamilton is quite right when he says that it is the policy of parliament to have the name given in cases of proposed amalgamation of railway companies, but it is not the policy of parliament to follow that rule in other cases.
Paragraph (h) of section 7 which gave this company the right to construct, acquire and operate other electric tramways, telegraph and telephone lines was considered so objectionable that it was struck out, but in considering subsection (f), as amended, which gives this company the right to acquire the business, good-will and property of any other company having similar objects, the committee took the view that that was not objectionable as it could only lead to amalgamation on a small scale and nothing in the nature of a monopoly injurious to the public.
Now, my hon. friend says that that creates a monopoly. But, suppose this is a steamship company, and there is a small steamship line operating in conjunction with them-an extension of their route-and they desire to buy it up and unite the two concerns. This would not be a monopoly or a policy to be discouraged. Of course, it is limited to the amount of its capital, and can only buy what its capital will purchase. The illustration I have given is a case that constantly happens with private individuals or corporations-two concerns engaged in similar lines unite; and. unless the union is of a very large amount of capital I do not see that there is anything in it in the nature of a monopoly. I sympathize with the object my hon. friend has in view and bear testimony to the fact that in the committee he takes the position that we should watch these things carefully. One of the greatest dangers of loose legis-

lation is in private Bills. Government Bills generally are scrutinized very carefully ; but private Bills sometimes pass without the care that should be bestowed upon them. Therefore, I am glad to welcome the expression of opinion of hon. gentlemen who look at these matters closely. But I think my hon. friend on further consideration will see that this does not involve the danger that he thinks it does.

I am not speaking with reference to this particular Bill or the gentlemen who are promoting it, but with regard to the general principle. The company will be a transportation company merely. But a railway company is a transportation company merely. It is hardly a case like that of one individual entering into partnership with another. Individuals have the right to do whatever a free man may do or whatever two or more persons m ly contract with each other to do. But these companies are creatures of parliament. This is a company with large capital and extensive power, its powers are not confined to the purchase of lines already in existence, for it is free to acquire all companies that may be formed hereafter and that would naturally come into competition with them. They may buy up such companies, and so deprive the public of the competition which is looked for. The principle for which I am contending is that that kind of thing should be guarded against. If the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) speaking on behalf of the government, thinks there is no objection to the clause I bow to his judgment. But it does seem to me that the principle that is applied to railway companies to prevent them from acquiring generally other railway companies should be applied to any corporation of this kind. If this company wants to acquire any existing steamship company, it is competent for parliament to consider whether it is reasonable that they should do so. But to give it a blanket authority, for all time, to acquire any company that may hereafter seek to carry on similar operations to those which this company is authorized to carry on, I think is a mistake.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). Wherever a number of persons ask to be incorporated as a company to carry on business not asking for any privileges from parliament other than that of incorporation, I think they should be left with the same powers and privileges as an individual has. Where a company has received special privileges, in the way of subsidies, grants or anything of that kind, the case is different. Under such conditions, it is quite right that the power should be reserved in a parliament. In the case of railway companies, previous' to the adoption of the
policy of granting subsidies, it was not thought necessary to impose these conditions that my hon. friend suggests, nor do I think it would be in the public interest to do so in this case. Banks are given great and special privileges
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: Are they authorized to amalgamate ?

Even they have power to amalgamate. But I cannot agree that it is in the best interest of the country and a benefit to business generally that, if men unite their capital to conduct business, they should be deprived of the ordinary privileges allowed to one individual or to several forming a partnership. It is not likely that they would exercise this power unless it were to the general advantage. I cannot imagine that there is more danger of a monopoly being brought about by giving these powers to a company like this than there is by leaving with an individual the power to purchase the business of another individual or the shares of a corporation.

I am always in favour of hampering anything that may be to the detriment of business, In this case a number of individuals are asking for a charter for a definite business, and have subscribed their own capital. They ask no privilege except that possessed by all people who are doing business. I can hardly agree, then, with my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that we should take power to prevent an amalgamation which would be allowed to individuals. It must be remembered that we have not in this country probably, too much capital. If it is necessary for a company like this to amalgamate with some other for the better carrying on of the business in which they are engaged, then, I think in tha interest of business and of the country, it is well that they would be allowed to do so. If it could be shown, as in the case of two great railway companies, that the amalgamation would have the effect of preventing competition I can understand that the country might step in and prevent it. But I do not think that a case has been made out to show that it is necessary that the country should be free to step in and prevent the amalgamation of another company with this one for the purpose of combining their resources in carrying on the business.
May I ask if section 9 as the Bill was originally printed stands as part of the Bill ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.

That gives this company the right to receive subsidy from the government or any person. Is it reasonable, if a company like this receives subsidies from the government, that they should have

power practically to use the money of tlie public to buy up competing concerns ?

The putting iu of this clause does not give them subsidies, but only gives them the power to receive them If they are given. And I fancy the company would have difficulty in getting subsidies. The power that gives them a subsidy, whether the Dominion, a province or a municipality, would make its own terms, which would properly be attached to the giving of the subsidy. There is no danger in this, for it simply says :	If you
can get a subsidy, you may enjoy it.

And it says also :	And
if you- get it and think that the way to enjoy it, you can use it to buy up other companies.

But my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) will see the broad difference between this Bill and legislation affecting railway companies. My hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) pointed out that to unite two railway companies would create a monopoly, because you cannot conveniently or without very great expense lay another railway alongside of it. But there is no monopoly whatever, iu uniting two steamship lines, for instance. If you amalgamate two steamship companies and you want another, you can easily get a charter for it. The conditions which would make a monopoly in the case of a railway do not exist in the case of an ordinary commercial company. The elements of monopoly are not in the latter ease.

This is the first time the clause which the hon. gentleman refers to has been brought to the notice of the Public Works Department, and in view of the absence of the hon. member who has charge of this Bill, I would ask that the Bill stand for consideration. This is a very important matter, seeing that the Bill practically declares that this river which is now navigable shall be made lion-navigable. Tlie^ interests involved are very great, and I desire a little time to have the officers of my department consider the matter and make a report upon it. I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.

Before the motion is put, I desire to say that I am a little surprised that the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill had not said something about it, or wired me on the subject. The city of Winnipeg is an important part of the province of Manitoba, but at the same

.time there are other parts of Manitoba of some importance. The dams and locks referred to in this Bill would cut the county of Selkirk, which I represent, almost entirely. Now the danger is this, that the Assiniboine river is a river of very low banks, not more than three or four feet; above high water mark at places, and an attempt is being made now to render that river navigable. Some six or eight months ago I urged the Public Works Department to sendl an engineer for the purpose of ascertaining if the crooks in that stream which dammed the water back could not be straightened out by making cuts. An engineer has gone up, I understand, and made a report on the navigability of the Assiniboine river, and in order to see what is required to make the river navigable. Last year the overflow of that stream caused damage in the city of Brandon, in Portage la Prairie, and the municipalities from Brandon down to Winnipeg of probably $450,000. A fair estimate made by the Board of Trade of Portage la Prairie gave the damage in the Portage municipality as $200,000. Between there and Brandon the damage would be probably $200,000. In the city of Brandon the water-works were washed away and great damage was done. Now this river will have to be improved, if not for the purpose of navigation, at least to prevent its banks overflowing. The Canadian Pacific Railway also were very seriously interfered with in their traffic, as the river flowed so far over its banks that it went up to the Canadian Pacific Railway track. In fact the old trail along the Assiniboine river was three feet and a half under water, the same trail that I travelled over twenty-three years ago. dry-shod. The water reached as high a level as the railways eight or ten miles east of Portage. So if we are going to allow the city of Winnipeg to put in locks at the city of Winnipeg that will interfere with navigation, or keep the water back, then they will certainly hear from the old settlers who reside along that river and from several other places further west beyond Brandon and Portage la Prairie. In regard to this canal also from the Assiniboine river to Lake Manitoba, using Long Lake as part of the channel, I presume that has been a work contemplated for the last twenty-four years, but nothing has been done. It is difficult to say what effect it will have on the waters of Lakes Manitoba and Winnipegosis. So if the scheme is carried out as proposed in this Bill it would affect a very large portion of the province of Manitoba. I would therefore ask the Minister of Public Works to have his engineer make a thorough report before he allows the city of Winnipeg either to throw a dam across the river at Winnipeg or to put in locks.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.

speechtext:
It Will be Leased for Fifty Years to the Grand Trunk Pacific.
And Running Rights Will be Granted to Other Railways-For the Western Sections a Guarantee of Bonds Will be Given
-Work to be at Once Rushed forward and Material to be Bought in Canada.
(Special Despatch to The Globe.)
Ottawa, July 2.-The main features of the government's policy in connection with the proposed transcontinental railway line have practically been determined, and it is expected that within a few days a contract with the Grand Trunk Company will be signed. The government undertake to construct a line from Moncton to Winnipeg via Quebec, and to lease it to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company for fifty years. For the first five years the company will pay no rental to the government. Foe the second five years they will pay the net surplus of receipts over working expenses. For the remaining forty years they agree to pay three per cent on the cost of construction.
The Western Section Guaranteed.
The government will guarantee the bonds for the stretch of line which the company themselves are to construct. In the case of the prairie section the guarantee will be 75 per cent of the actual cost of construction, but is not to exceed $13,000 a mile. The'government have arbitrarily fixed 500 miles as the length of the mountain section, and for this distance the guarantee will also be 75 per cent of the actual cost up to a maximum of $30,000 a mile.
The rates to be charged are to be subject to the control of the Governor in Council or the railway commission, but on the government section of the line the rates are not to be cut down to a figure that will prevent the company from paying the annual rental.
Running Rights Provided For.
Other railway companies are to be granted running rights over the Winnipeg-Jfoncton section. This is to be a matter of mutual agreement, and in the event of failure to arrive at a friendly understanding, the government will prescribe the terms, subject, of course, to the rights which the Grand Trunk Pacific possess as lessees and operators of the line.
Materials Used to be Canadian.
In view of the government constructing the eastern section of the railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company have reduced their capital from $75,000,000 to $45,000,000. The company, as an evidence of good faith, will deposit $5,000,000 ir the Bank of Montreal in cash or approved securities. As far as possible the materials used in the construction are to be of Canadian manufacture. The government have made a point of stipulating that, wherever it could be done, the articles that enter into construction should be bought in Canada, and the company readily agreed to this. A majority of the di rectors mu3t be resident in Canada. Mr. C. M. Hays is to be president of the company, and Mr. Wainwright, vice-president. Among the directors will be one of the Rothschilds-probably Lord Rothschild, the head of the great financial house-Lord Welby, Sir Charles Rivers Wilson and Mr. Arthur Smithers.
To Rush the Work Forward.
Mr. Hays and his associates are in earnest in the desire to begin construction and push the work to completion as rapidly as possible. ******
Sixty Survey Parties Out.
The company have sixty survey parties out at present, of whom ten are working between Lake Abbittibbi and Quebec.

speechtext: This vote was granted in 1901-2. The amount lapsed, but the work was gone on with, and we are asking this vote to pay for the work done during the past year.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: How did the amount lapse ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: It was voted and the work was not completed the 30th June, a year ago, so the vote lapsed.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Why did you not make provision last session ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
There was an amount voted last session, but it was not sufficient.

speechtext: Tills is to make provision for paying the contribution to the local government of New Brunswick, not exceeding half the sum spent by them from 1895 to 1902 in the construction of wharfs in the St. John river.
