subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: When was the arrangement made ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I have forgotten the date, but it was when Hon. Mr. Foster was Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The vote was given for this amount previously, but, owing to some difference between the Auditor General and the parties, it has never been paid. This is to pay the amount in full.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I suppose the real objection on the part of the Auditor General was that he was not satisfied that the amount for the wharfs was correct.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: No ; as I am informed, the dispute was as to the form of the vote. The Auditor Gene-eral held that, as the money was voted, it could not be paid to the provincial government. Hon. gentlemen will note the form of this vote, which is ' amount due to local government.' That not having been in the previous vote the Auditor General said the money could not be paid over.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Then, if I understand the minister correctly there has been an agreement between the Dominion government and the local government as to these particular wharfs built from 1895 to 1902, that we should pay one-half the cost ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Yes, that is practically correct.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: And the only trouble was that the Auditor General thought the amounts should be paid to the contractor instead of to the local government.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: That is hardly it. He was not satisfied that, with the vote in the form in which it was formerly passed, the money could be paid to the local government. There is no doubt about money having been spent on the various works.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
Spent by the local government ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. Yes.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Is that the total amount paid by this government under this arrangement since 1895 ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is the amount due since 1895, but not the total amount paid. An amount was paid year after year under this arrangement, but it must have been going on for several years up to 1895, when exception was taken to it by the Auditor General, and since that time it has never been rectified. This is to pay all that has accrued from 1895 to 1902 to the provincial government.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: What is the total amount expended by this government on wharfs on the St. John river and its tributaries, leaving out the city of St. John ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
I had a statement here for the main estimates, but I haven't it at hand at the moment. I will bring the information down.
Harbours and rivers-Quebec, Cacouna-extension of wharf, $1,350.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is to pay for some materials purchased in connection with this wharf for the current year.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I suppose that this wharf was built for the accommodation of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company. What return do we get for the money expended on such a wharf ? I am a little interested in these points because we in Ontario occasionally make a request for public expenditure on such works. For instance, in Toronto we sometimes want something done on our harbour, but find it difficult to get it. But when I go down to Cacouna, which is a pleasure resort, I find a large aniount spent for a wharf for the benefit, as I take it, of the Richelieu and Ontaria Navigation Company. What does that company contribute ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is a public wharf, but I suppose it is used by the steamers of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company. It was originated, however, for the benefit of the public, and I take it that it was because the wharf was there that the company's steamers called. I understand that the greatest influence in bringing about the construction of this wharf was that of one of our most influential statesmen, the late respected leader of the Conservative government, Sir John Macdonald, who had a residence there.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken. Sir John lived at Riviere du Loup, not at Cacouna.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, r might be mistaken on that point, but the information in the department is that the work was started as the result of his in-

fluence in the first place. I do not s'ay that it was not the proper thing to do, but 1 am explaining to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock), in answer to his question, how the wharf came to be built. I do not think it was built at the instance, or for the benefit of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I think it was built for the benefit of the hotel that was constructed there by a company, and I do not see why the government should build a wharf for the benefit of such a concern. It is not to accommodate a section of the country with a large population, but simply to promote a summer resort.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) is mistaken. There is a large district served by this wharf. At any rate, the Dominion, for many years, has followed the plan of building these wharfs, and, unless we change our policy I suppose we shall have to continue building these wharfs to some extent.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I do not wish to be misunderstood. If the respected head of the government some years ago, the late right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald recommended that this should be built and maintained by and at the public expense, make no mistake about it, I would asquiesce, for I know that he would not have recommended it unless it were to the public interest.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I believe the hon. minister is mistaken in saying that the Richelieu boats go there. They may go there but only occasionally. Cacouna is visited only by people who go to spend the summer there.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Morin) allow me ? I misunderstood the information furnished me by the engineer. I understood him to say that the steamers stop there, but I was mistaken. The whqrf is altogether for the benefit of the people who reside there regularly or as visitors.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The people who go there to spend the summer are generally rich people, and, if they want wharf accommodation they should provide it themselves. There is a railway there, and people can go down and up by rail. But sometimes they engage a steamer at Quebec and take the trip by water for pleasure. If they enjoy these pleasure trips, they should pay for them. The poorer class of people realize no benefit whatever from this wharf.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Would the hon. minister tell us the size of the wharf-I see that this item is for an extension.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The wharf is 977 feet long, 24 feet wide and the mean height is 17 feet, and 24 feet wide.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: How much has been expended on it up to the present time by the government.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The total is $26,611.60.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Would the hon. minister explain why the wharf has to be extended ? One would imagine that it was quite large enough for the business.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
They want deeper water to allow the larger
class of steamers to reach the wharf. However, this amount has been expended, the material was purchased, and this is to pay for it.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Does the minister know for a fact that any business was done there other than we have learned from the hon. member who has just spoken ? I do not object to spending money to aid people to get in their commodities or to get them out, but I think we should draw the line at a mere pleasure resort for wealthy people going up there from Quebec to spend the summer. I object to spending $25,000 or $30,000 of the people's hard-earned money to benefit a few pleasure seekers. I feel a little sore about this, when I remember that in my riding there are five or six wharfs of more importance ; one of them, Presqu'Isle harbour, one of the best'in Ontario, where millions of bushels of grain have been shipped, and not a dollar of public money has been spent all along that shore. Does the minister know whether there is any need at all for this work ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: There is no doubt that the wharf is largely used in the summer time by the class of people to which the hon. gentleman has referred. I think also it is used a good deal by people in that district to ship their produce over to the north shore. This is in the county of T6miscouata.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Is there any revenue from that wharf ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: There is no revenue. The government owns the wharf.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: If the people wanted a wharf and the government owned it and they exacted any tolls, there ought to be a revenue ; and if there is no revenue and the government own that wharf, it is quite evident that there is something wrong. If there was business done over that wharf, and it was conducted on business principles, we should have some revenue from it.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: There is a large number of these wharfs that have never been transferred to the Marine Department.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
There is a wharf only six miles above there, at Rivifire du Loup, where

the steamboats belonging to the Richelieu Navigation Company land. AH the boats going up and down the St. Lawrence stop at that wharf. On the north shore, almost opposite, is the mouth of the Saguenay river, and right opposite Caeouna is what is called Red Island, a very dangerous place for navigation. No boats of any kind dare go to Caeouna except special boats. All the business done is transacted at Rivi&re du Loup wharf. So that you can see at once that the wharf is of no use except for the purposes I have mentioned before. I do not see why the government should spend the people's money in that way. There are other places needing a wharf more than that place.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Did the engineer of the department go down and examine this place, and report that such extension and repairs were required ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Yes, that was done. This was a work on which the previous government had spent at least $20,000, and it would be poor policy to allow that work to go to pieces when a small expenditure will keep it up. I cannot admit this work is of no use. It may be, as the hon. gentleman says, an advantage to people who reside there in the summer. But it is a great advantage to have these people, mostly foreigners, perhaps, reside there during the summer season. But when I find a work for which $20,000 had been voted by the previous government without criticism, I think it is the duty of the department to keep that in proper repair.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: But there is also an extension.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: There was a small extension added in making the repairs, an extension of about 50 feet, so that schooners could use the wharf.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: My objection is not to the expenditure of $1,350, but there is a principle involved. The government are spending the money of this country in building a wharf, and we ask upon what principle they are proceeding. Are they doing it in the interest of the general public or in the interest of some private company ? I contend that if this is not in the general interest of Canada, it must be in the interest of a hotel company, and that is something to which we should draw the minister's attention. If in the past this country has foolishly spent money on this work, there is no reason why we should go on spending money upon it. If that place is worth building a wharf upon, the Richelieu & Ontario Company will spend that $1,350 or more, if necessary. If it is not worth their while to do it, it is not worth the while of this government to do it. Let the companies who are making money out of it spend their money in keeping up this wharf.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I do not agree with what the minister said just now. He said that the late government had built a wharf there. That is correct. But you must remember that you have condemned the late government and voted them out of power for their bad conduct. Now, what are we to think of you when you turn round and do things just as bad, or worse ? If the late government has done wrong, do not follow their example; draw a line and quit that kind of business.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: We have not heard from the minister any answer to the request of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) as to the principle on which the government are proceeding in building wiharfs of this kind. It seems to me there ought to be some well defined principle for giving grants to wharfs. There are many wharfs on our lakes and rivers, and on our ocean inlets, on some of which large sums have been expended, and on others nothing has been expended.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The policy has been to build wharfs where-ever they are considered to be in the public interest. We must admit that the public money has been pretty widely distributed. Applications are numerous, and it is not possible to meet them all. But this is not a new work, it is an old work, and I do not know that it comes under any new policy. As I have said on several occasions, as long as it is the policy of parliament to build these wharfs, I suppose it will remain in the discretion of the government to say what wharfs they will build in the public interest. I do not think that this work is subject to severe criticism, in view of the fact that it has been established for so long a time, and that the residents in that district have pressed for improvements.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Here is something I cannot understand. Here are $34,526 asked for. What is the use bf our criticising one item ? You come here and you want $1,300 to extend that wharf. We prove to you that the wharf is of no use, and while you hear us you do not pay any attention to us at all. You just do as you please. If you are going to do so, why not pass this item in full, $34,000, and be done with it ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The hon. member who represents Temis-couata (Mr. Gauvreau) says that the people in that district take a very different view from that of the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I will bet you they do.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
And the difficulty is to decide betweeu the hon. gentlemen as to the necessity of this work.
Hull-completion of wharf, including freight shed, $3,200.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is in settlement in full of the contract.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I see that this work has been going on since 1900. In 1900-1901 the government paid $9,460 on this work. In 1901-2 they paid $40,977.59 upon it. Perhaps the hon. minister can tell us what they paid under the appropriation of last year ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The total amount paid on the work was $52,042.71.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I make it $53,637, but the difference is not very material. These items came up in this way year after year. I have called attention to it in the railway estimates. We never know when we pass an estimate for a public work whether we are authorizing what is going to complete the work or simply throwing in so much on account. I want once again to protest against this manner of conducting public business. I cannot say what occurred in 1900, but year after year items are passed for public* works without the explanation which ought to be given. Will the hon. minister assure us that this really completes the business ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This will complete the work.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Really the figures are rather appalling. We are not very far from Hull, and we are able to judge of the amount of money we have expended, and we want to know what benefit we are going to get from it. Does the honl minister assume to say that this country is getting a return for an expenditure of $50,000 on a work of that kind ? I can understand that it may be an advantage to lumbermen and other people who make money out of it, but what is the Dominion government getting out of it ? Are we getting 3 per cent on the money we have expended ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: It is impossible to give any idea of the revenue. The work has just been finished, and it will be transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries at the end of another year, and if there is any revenue to be derived from it we will know then. At the present time, it has not been transferred, and there has been no revenue derived.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The statement of the hon. minister confirms the report that was in circulation at the time of the appointment of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prgfontaine) that all these public wharfs were to be transferred to the Marine Department.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Ever since the Marine Department has been established, these wharfs, when completed, have always been transferred to the Marine Department.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Will the hon. minister be good enough to tell the committee whether any steamboats carrying passengers ever go to that wharf at Hull ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I only give the hon. gentleman the information that I have, which is that the Ottawa River Navigation Company use that wharf. It is the intention to run the ferry between Ottawa and Hull from that wharf.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Is it not unusual to build freight sheds on wharfs ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: In a great many places it is usual to build freight sheds on these wharfs.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: It is not unusual, but it is very improper.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is a good work, whether a justifiable one or not, I do not know.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: These freight houses are not constructed on all wharfs. How does the hon. minister select the particular wharfs on which to build freight sheds ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
In some of these smaller places freight sheds have been built for the accommodation of the public. It depends a great deal on the conditions in the locality where the public wharf is constructed. In most places corporations and private individuals get the privilege of building right on the wharf, or on the adjoining property.
Isle Grosbois, opposite Boueherville-dredging channel, $5,151.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is to pay for the dredging done there during the past year. This is the full amount that was spent there and it is in payment of the work done.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: This is special dredging, because around there last year and years before the government have done a great deal of dredgirg in the main channel, but the dredging at this island must be special dredging for a special channel.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Yes, this is special work ordered by the Minister of Public Works. There was no appropriation made, and this is to pay the people who did the work.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
I see this work was not begun this year by accident. It was begun tin 1900. The Canadian Construction, Limit-(ed, received $4,039 upon it in 1901-2, and although there was no appropriation asked from parliament for further expenditure last year, the department appears to have gone on and authorized the continuance of the work, and incurred a liability of over $5,000. This

is another specimen of what we had up in connection with the Galops canal, where two years ago some $50,000 was expended by the government without any authority whatever from parliament. At the end of the year we had the most extraordinary statement made that the work had been proceeded with without the authority of the head of the department, and yet an engineer and a gang of men were supervising the work the whole season. The minister says that this present work was proceeded with last year without authority of parliament, and yet we are asked to pay $5,000 now for it. This is an extraordinary way of conducting the business of the country. I appeal to the minister whether that is going to continue. Are we to give carte bianche to the minister to spead any money he likes, and then allow him to come here for a vote of indemnity ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I do not ask that we should have carte blanche. I do not approve of the system. I think it unfortunate that this thing should occur. I have to ask for several similar items to pay accounts fbr which no appropriation has been authorized, and some of them I think are perfectly warranted and could be justified and I would be willing to take the responsibility for them. As to the others they were authorized by the minister. These people have done the work in good faith and they perhaps had no means of knowing that there was no appropriation by parliament and that it was not authorized. The Premier, I suppose, and the government have to take the responsibility, but I do not know that they had any more knowledge that this was going on than had the hon. member for Hamilton.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: It is the country that is taking the responsibility. The country has to pay it. If the minister himself paid it we do not care who would take the responsibility.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: The minister authorized this work without an appropriation and I do not think it would be right for us to repudiate the amounts. The work was probably well done. I am not pretending to defend or approve of the system of spending money without authority.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
This work was done under the responsibility of a member of the government of which the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) is a very important minister. The whole country has to take the responsibility because the whole country has to pay it. From the minister's own statement the government is deserving of censure for being derelict in their duty in allowing any minister to spend money without the authority of this parliament. So far as we on this side of the House are concerned, we repudiate the responsibility Mr. BARKER.
and we enter a strong and vigorous protest against that kind of thing being done. Even the minister himself will not pretend to defend this thing. The government has no right to ask us to vote money in this kind of way. If a minister has done this on his individual responsibility, he should be made individually responsible for it.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: I am afraid you would have a poor lookout for getting it back.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Some time ago a gentleman from Quebec was here when we were voting money for public works, and after the House adjourned he complained to me that they could not get one dredge in or around Quebec. He pointed out that vessels could not get to some of the wharfs on account of the sand and gravel banks and that the trade of the port was greatly hampered. That gentleman asked me to mention this to the Minister of Public Works the next time the House was in Committee of Supply, and I avail of this opportunity of doing so.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: There is a small dredge at Quebec but I do not think she is large enough to do deep dredging. However, with a view of getting value for our money we have asked parliament to be kind enough to give a grant of $75,000 for the purpose of purchasing a dredge that would be able to do the work at Quebec and below Quebec.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: In addition to this sum of $5,151. I suppose you have not taken into account the $20,000 or $30,000 which would be represented by the use of the dredge in doing this work. Do you keep a separate account for these dredges showing day by day the work they do and their expenses. Is this an additional amount to that ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
This work was done by contract. An account is kept of the work done by the government dredges, the cost of each dredge and all that sort of thing. The expense of these dredges is as a rale paid out of the vote for maintenance of dredges belonging to the government.
River St. Maurice-dredging eastern entrance of channel. $555.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: It is a justifiable work, and the vote is for a small overdraft.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Is it outside of the jurisdiction of the Three Rivers commissioners.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
The jurisdiction of the Three Rivers harbour commissioners extends only to the St. Lawrence. This work was done at the junction of the St. Lawrence and the St. Maurice rivers, where there are large mills and where barges come to load lumber. This work was urg-

ent during the spring because then they were splitting their booms and a dredge could not enter after the booms were put down. The water is sometimes too low there to float the logs. I requested the government to do this work in the interest of the lumber trade of Three Itivers which asked for it.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: Are they dredging the river so as to be able to float logs ?

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.
speechtext: They dredged the mouth of the St. Lawrence to allow boats to come in to load lumber. What I said was that there was not water enough to float logs at certain seasons of the year.

subtopic: A GOVERNMENT RAILWAY FROM MONCTON TO WINNIPEG.

of Marine and Fisheries as well as the hon. Minister of Public Works to these docks on the Georgian bay and particularly on the north shore. There is a line of steamboats calling at Bruce Mines, Cockburn Island, Thessalon and other places, and while the country has spent on an average from $20,000 to $25,000 erecting a dock at each one of these places, these steamboat owners are permitted to call at these docks upon which storehouses are erected and what is the result ? We will take the case of Thessalon, where there has been an expenditure of $20,000 or $25,000. The Dominion government did not derive a single cent revenue from that dock last year. The country goes to an expense of $20,000 or $30,000 for building these docks and after they are finished you permit a wealthy steamboat company to use them and to store their freight in the storehouses while the country is not collecting a single dollar at the thriving town of Thessalon. Under the Post Office Act, it is provided that the salaries of postmasters shall be contingent upon the revenue of their respective post offices, but for many years the late government did not appear to think that that created a legal liability, and failed to increase the salaries of some of the postmasters. The question came up, however, in the case of the postmaster at Winnipeg. Inasmuch as the practice had been to disregard that provision and not look upon it as creating any legal liability, I did not depart from that practice but allowed the salaries to continue at the old rate. However, Mr. Hargraft preferred to take the opinion of the court upon the subject, and brought an action in the Exchequer Court. The court held that the postmasters were entitled legally to the increase based upon the percentage. If hon. gentlemen will refer to the Civil Service List, page 208, they 186
will find the schedule under the head ' city postmasters ' with a provision :
When postage collections exceed $250,000, $4,000.
When postage collections are from $200,000 to $250,000, $3,750.

It has happened that, in the course of years, the revenues of city post offices have gradually increased, but the salaries of the postmasters and assistant postmasters have not increased according to this scale. While the winter service boats were running the mails arriving at Georgetown, and at Summerside also, had to wait ten or twelve hours before they w.ere distributed from the west to Charlottetown, or from Georgetown to Charlottetown and Summerside. Passengers arriving there thirty or forty at a time had to telegraph to Charlottetown and to put up money out of their own pockets to get special trains in order to reach the capital. These trains paid for by private individuals carried His Majesty's mails free of cost. This matter has been going on for a number of years. I believe some of the ministers disclaim having had any notice of it this last winter: but if they will turn up the ' Hansard ' of last winter and the winter before, they will find that reference was made to this matter. My hon. friend from Queen's. Prince Edward Island (Mr. MacKinnon) puts me in mind of the time when I crossed myself. We had thirty or forty passengers on board the steamer, arriving about six o'clock. We wired to the board of trade and to the hon. member for Queen's, and through his good offices, who put up the money from his own pocket, we finally got a train. There may be something in the grievance that the bon. member (Mr. Lefurgey) has just mentioned in some small sections of the country in Prince Edward Island, but I do not wish the committee to be under a wrong impression about tlie mail service of Prince Edward Island. In regard to the winter mail service, the grievance of which the hon. member speaks, arose from the desire on the part of the government to comply with the wishes of his own constituents. At bis own request, and at the request of the people of Sum-merside and Prince county, they put the steamer ' Stanley ' on the winter route between Cape Tormentine and Summerside. The ' Stanley ' stuck in the ice and she remained there during the greater part of the winter. Another steamer was sent to her relief and she also remained there during a large part of the winter, and while both steamers were fast in the ice, the mail service was not as good last winter as it had been formerly. It arose from the fact that there was more ice in the straits than usual and a desire to please the people of Prince county, who urged upon the government the desirability of sending the ' Stanley ' to the western part of the island. These people are represented by members of the opposition. Members supporting the government in the House were desirous that they should be fairly treated and they yielded to the request, and that is the reason why tliis service was established. The bon. member, time and again, has spoken of this winter service across the straits, both as to the steamers and the mail service. I rise particularly to point out that Prince Edward Island is not ice bound all the year round. We have passed the middle of the summer ; yet, the bon. member still reiterates bis statements about the ice thus advertising our province as a place unfit to live in. It conveys a wrong impression to the world. This is one of the most fertile spots in the Dominion, and one of the most progressive, and it is one where the hon. Postmaster General has improved the mail service far beyond anything in the history of that province. Both locally and from an interprovincial point of view be has improved the service greatly. I regret to hear lion, members coming from the province talking in this way of Prince Edward Island. I have looked up the record of ' Hansard ' and I find that for 20 or 30 years hon. members from the island have got up and continued discussing this ice question, and they give people the impression that we are nearer to the north pole than we are. It is true that we have ice in the winter, but the government has placed two steamers on the

service where the former government had but one. These hon. gentlemen have been chasing a tunnel project which would cost almost half the value of the whole province instead of doing what they could do to secure an improved service. They have been getting up and grumbling about the matter and suggesting no remedy. They get up and chase that tunnel scheme that would cost $10,000,000 or $20,000,000, instead of in a practical way proposing some feasible scheme. Hon. gentlemen get up year in and year out and continue the same old story about the ice. There is no reason to talk in that manner. A few of these grievances occurred last winter, and I have explained the reason why. So far as the salaries of postmasters on the island are concerned, there are a few places where they should be increased a little, and I am satisfied that if the question is brought to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General this will be done. I suppose he is treating the island in the same way as he is treating other parts of Canada, and I think we should be satisfied with that. It is not a money making transaction to keep a post office any way. The people of Prince Edward Island are generally satisfied with the service, and although this trouble did occur last winter, it was through the fact that an experiment was being made in the western route during a winter when navigation was more difficult than for the past twenty years.

The question under discussion is of so much importance to the people of Prince Edward Island that I cannot allow it to pass without making a few observations, especially at this early hour of the morning. I regret that the Postmaster General so cavalierly brushed aside the grievances of my hon. friend from Prince. He said that some slight difficulty occurred last winter and it was removed, and he trusted the like would never occur again. A slight difficulty ! Why the people of Prince Edward Island were for weeks at a time deprived of their mail, and the government of Canada were too mean and too contemptibly small to hire a special train to send these mails to their destination when they arrived on the soil of Prince Edward Island. Sir, when the island entered the union a solemn compact was entered into by the government of Canada that we should have steam communication continuously between the island and the mainland for the convenience of mails and passengers. The Postmaster General says a slight delay occurred last year. Let me tell him that the people of Prince Edward Island were filled with indignation from one end of it to the other. They were on the verge of revolt. This mass meeting was held in the citadel of the hon. member for East Queen's ; held there under-I was going to say under his nose-but within the length of his arin. The board of trade of the city of Charlottetown passed strong resolutions and sent a delegation to this government asking redress of the grievances. My hon. friend has spoken about ice, but let him read the speech of the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey) when it appears in * Hansard ' to-morrow, and he will see that the hon. gentleman made no reference whatever to the ice He wanted to make it appear that the whole trouble was in connection witli the ice, and he says we have fine weather now and that we should not give the province a bad name by talking about ice. speechtext: We are dealing now with what occurred last winter. I think the difficulty was largely due to the fact that the government listened too much to the representations of the western part of the island and went too far in trying to meet the wishes of everybody. 1 believe that in that they made a mistake, and I trust that that mistake will not be repeated. I think that the ministers, and particularly the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, has information that will enable him to place the winter steamers on the route that will give the people of Prince Edward Island the best service. And 1 believe that next year, and for the years to come, there will be no great cause for complaint. There was a difficulty and we might as well recognize it. There was a steamer plying between Pictou and Georgetown and one between Cape Tor-mentine and Summerside. It was ce'rtainly difficult for the railway department to provide trains to meet both steamers on their arrival, for they did not arrive on schedule time, and no one could say when they would be in. That difficulty will continue as long as the steamers are on different routes. If they are put upon one route, the one known to be feasible, the one the use of which for the last thirty years has resulted in a reasonable service, it will be easy for the Railway Department to meet the steamers and to convey passengers and mails to Charlottetown where they may be distributed to their destinations. The government, in their anxiety to please everybody, particularly the people of the western part of the island, made a mistake. It is no reflection upon the harbour of Summerside to say that it cannot be a winter port. Montreal cannot be a winter port, yet it is a very important city. It is a fact known to men skilled in winter navigation that Summerside cannot be successfully navigated in the winter, and so the route between Cape Tormeutine and Summerside cannot be successfully maintained. But the route between Georgetown and Pictou has been fairly successful since it was established about thirty years ago. With the two boats on that route, a satisfactory service will be given to the people. I trust that idea will be followed. I believe the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will be seized of the facts and will carry on the service in a way satisfactory to all parties concerned.

In the case of the Inverness Railway, I regret to observe that nothing has been done. The Postmaster General is evidently seeking to make both ends meet between revenue and expenditure in his department; but of all the departments, I believe this particular department is the one that the people of Canada would be willing to pay deficits to keep in a satisfactory condition.
Leaving the railway question and dwelling a little on this economy in the mail service, I wish to call attention to the fact that so much economy was practiced in the county of Inverness last winter that while travelling on a train I happened to fall in with the deputy post office inspector for Nova Scotia, and he told me, to my amazement, that he was just going down to Inverness to seek for offers to convert about half the daily mail service in that county into a tri-weekly service. Needless to say that I felt quite excited over the evidence of retrogression in this connection. I must say en passant that the Postmaster General was not at home at the time. But now that he is here and that I am here, I wish to call his attention to the fact that on that occasion tenders were publicly asked to have about half daily mail service in Inverness converted into a tri-weekly one, As usual the Minister of Finance was at his post, and I appealed to him in the absence of the Postmaster General ; and I wish to say here to-night that if the officials of the Postmaster General had their way, and had it not been for the prompt action of the Minister of Finance, the county of Inverness to-day would be jogging along, so to speak, with a tri-weekly service where it had a daily mail service for 35 years previously. I, therefore, feel that I would be derelict in my duty if I did not call public attention to a matter which threatened to affect so seriously a matter of vital interest to the county of Inverness, which perhaps of all counties in Canada is progressing the most rapidly. At such a time, then I submit whether such a handicap would not be a most regrettable circumstance. I asked a question in this House last year as to the comparative cost of carrying the mails in the county of Inverness in the year 1896 and in the year 1902. The Postmaster General's answer to that showed that there had been $5,000 a year for six years saved out of the mail service in the county of Inverness by the Post Office Department. I would not complain about that were it not that I find it very difficult to secure any improvement * in the old order of things with regard to the

mall service in that county. The matter has been progressing, however, as 1 said before. Other departments of this government are doing well for that county, and X regret all the more that this particular department of the government should do anything which would calculate to retard the progress of that county.

The hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes) has referred to the service between Georgetown and Pictou as being the only service that proved satisfactory. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if there was not a period last year when the captain himself reported that for upwards of two weeks it was impossible to enter the harbour of Pictou. I want further to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the report of the resident engineer, to show how up-to-date this government has been in providing a suitable service. I am going back to the year 1894. This letter is dated March 15, 1901:
Sir.-I returned to the office from Richibucto just before mail time yesterday, and on opening your letter despatched immediately a copy I had on hand of my report made on the 14th of February, 1894, on Cape Traverse and Carle-ton Point. Since that date other references to the same subject have occurred in several reports of mine relating to Cape Tormentine, the harbour intended to be the New Brunswick end of the island crossing.
I inclose an extract from report No. 4039, dated 'the 8th of September last, which in a condensed form points out the facilities for successful winter navigation presented by the narrows of Northumberland strait. I beg you to read this in conjunction with the report of 1894, forwarded yesterday.
This report was made in 1894, that Carle-ton Point was the place to establish a pier for a winter service, and we have now the engineer of the government going over the same ground again and using this as an excuse for not going on with the pier.
The primary work of the examination made in 1894 was intended to determine whether a harbour should be made at Cape Traverse. As you will see, the conclusion is obvious that Cape Traverse is utterly unsuitable, while Carleton Point presents undoubtedly the best site for a harbour of the island side of the strait. One question has arisen since the date of that report, namely, objection has been made to- crossing from Cape Tormentine because of the risk a steamer would run of being swept upon the point of Jouriman reef. To this it may be said that in the present crossing from Pictou to Georgetown the Caribou shoals constitute a similar danger ; while the area of those shoals is, from their appearance on the chart, perhaps larger than the area of Jouriman reef, the dangerous part of which may be almost limited to that point.
Besides, if there is any danger of a steamer being carried on Jouriman reef it can only happen while the current is setting westward, and would be entirely removed when the tide stream ran to eastward. As you know, the flood stream that enters Northumberland strait from both ends, the two tides meeting and parting abreast Cape Tormentine and Tyrone. Of course, in ice Mr. Mclennan.
navigation, or in open navigation, much depends upon the skill and judgment of the mariner. Since the strait is so narrow at this point some opportunity for observation of the conditions of the crossing will be given from the masthead of the steamer before starting, an advantage not found at Pictou. A short time ago the 'Stanley' was drifting about in the ice oil Pictou for fifteen lays, and a few years ago was in similar case for sixteen days. Such a contingency would not I think be posible where the current runs, where the ice is not merely moving, but is parted east and west by the tides twice a day.

Resident Engineer.
I have another report of the resident engineer dated 8th September, 1900, in which he says :
It is, I believe, admitted that daily communication by steam is the object sought. Hitherto that object has not been obtained during the winter months. Up to this time the winter steamer has been crossing from Pictou to Georgetown, a distance of about forty-two miles, with more or less irregularity occasioned by the ice. The northwest winds of the winter drive the field ice to the eastern end of the strait of Northumberland and sometimes lodge it against the Cape Breton shore, completely blocking the eastern end of the passage at which Georgetown and Pictou are situated. When the ice is packed as in this manner it is almost impossible for a steamer to force her way through, as will be seen from the following quotation from Admiral Makaroff's description of the voyage of the Yermak' (vide the proceedings of the Royal Geographical Society for January, 1900), who found it easier to break the ice in the polar seas with that vessel than in the Baltic, because in the Arctic seas the ice is broken, while in *he Baltic it extended from land to land.
The engineer is pointing out one of the main difficulties in the navigation of the straits at the eastern end of the island. The ice is carried in an easterly direction and is jammed up between Pictou island and the Cape Breton shore, and where there is no room for relief it is impossible for these steamers to break through. He points out further that the tides meet and part twice daily at the Capes and this forms loose ice which it is very much easier for the boats to get through. He goes on :
Floes of ice might be several miles or several fathoms in length. Between the ice floes are the lanes, which are very irregular. Sometimes ice floes are pressed against each other and sometimes not. When the ice is not pressed, the progress of the ship is very easy. Floes of ice even a mils long move away and give pass-

age to the ship. But, the fact is that even ice 14 feet thick cracks when charged at by the ship, provided there is room to remove broken parts.
In the neighbourhood of Cape Tormentine the two branches of the principle tide wave, which formed at the Magdalen Island into the east and west ends of the strait respectively (but with 12 hours difference of time) meet each other with a surface overrun in either direction according to the moon's age, due to the diurnal inequality. Thus, in the neighbourhood of Cape Tormentine the currents meet and part twice a day.
What he means by this is that the tide forms off the Magdalen Island and it flows in at the eastern end of the island and up around the western end, coming in at both ends and meeting the Capes twice daily.
This condition is of course favourable to the loosening of any blocked ice there might be. But there are really two considerations which recommend a winter crossing from Cape Tormentine :
1.	Cape Tormentine is the nearest point to Prince Edward Island, the distance across being only 8 miles, and it is certain, the voyage being dangerous, the shorter the passage the better. I believe the distance to Georgetown is 42 miles through ice more closely packed than at Cape Tormentine.
2.	That the narrowest part of the strait is found the strongest current and current assists in loosening the ice.
These are two elementary principles that I do not think the hon. member for King's can contradict.
There are other ice crossings in northern Europe somewhat similar to that between Cape Tormentine and Prince Edward Island in the winter. One of these between Zealand and Funen in the great belt, appears to resemble very strongly in many respects that of Cape Tormentine and illustrates the fact that at least in Denmark the principle of adopting the shortest, passage has been observed. This crossing has been maintained I believe except in one severe winter (when detention for a day or two occurred), without interruption. The steamers start from Neibor, in the island of Funen, a harbour of which Knuds Head is the headland. From Knuds Head to Korsor in Zealand, a distance of 10 nautical miles, is the passage. The great belt must be more hazardous in the winter than Northumberland strait at Cape Tormentine because of the number of reefs and shoals. The prevailing current in the great belt is northward but variable and occasionally the streams and eddies are locally very strong.
Here we find away up in Denmark that the people get an almost uninterrupted service. In one season there was one day whicli they could not cross, while here we are in Canada, with only eight miles to cross and the hon. member for Queen's has spoken of it as being a fairly reasonable service when our boats are in the ice for fifteen or sixteen days at a stretch.
The shortest crossing of Northumberland strait would be from Cape Tormentine to Carle-ton Point but there is no harbour at the latter place. The distance to Summerside is about six-te6n	hut it is wise to try first whether
uninterrupted communications can be main* tained between Cape Tormentine and Summer-side during the winter, because, if so, construction of an expensive artificial harbour at Carleton Point may be avoided. Of course there is a disposition always to accept whatever is as immutable and in changing the establishment of anything that has become worthily or unworthily by lapse of time and institution, local prejudices will be met. Careful consideration should be given however to the experiment of crossing from Cape Tormentine.
In selecting the crossing for the steamer at the Strait of Canso, where heavy ice is found in the winter, I chose the point on the Cape Breton shore nearest to the Nova Scotian terminus of the railway. This crossing afterwards adopted by the Intercolonial Railway has I understand, proved satisfactory, and may perhaps afford another illustration of the principle that the shortest ice crossing is liable to be the best.
Tours obediently,
*	(Sgd.) E. T. P. SHEWEN,
Resident Engineer.
